speaker: Narrator
old: The hearth smells of spiced cider and wet wool, though the woman behind the polished bar smells of lavender water and brass coin.
new: The hearth smells of spiced cider, and the woman behind the bar smells of lavender water and brass coin.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: Step in out of the damp, my dears, and mind the mud on the runner. You have the look of guests who can afford a hot bath and a proper bed.
new: Mind the mud on the runner, my dears. You look like guests who can afford a hot bath and a bed.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: Single room is one gold piece, a triple is two, and both come with a hot bath and breakfast at Twilight. We have a stage for players and four sturdy beasts in the stable if the road calls.
new: Single room is one gold piece, a triple is two, with a hot bath and Twilight breakfast. We have a stage for players and four beasts in the stable.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: Wickermoor runs on custom and small favors, darlings. Keep on the right side of Mayor Somerton's paperwork, pay your tab before dawnless morning, and the Green Queen will smile on you.
new: Keep on the right side of Mayor Somerton's paperwork, pay your tab before dawnless morning, and the Green Queen will smile on you, darlings.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: Half the parish has been coughing up marsh-damp, and two lads from the south lane never came home from the heather. Bad for tempers, wonderful for the sale of hot toddies.
new: Half the parish is coughing up marsh-damp, and two south lane lads never came home from the heather. Bad for tempers, wonderful for hot toddy sales.

speaker: Narrator
old: Silver hares with tiny branched antlers swing from her ears, and beside her account ledger sits a cracked leather book stained with dried sap.
new: Silver hares with tiny antlers swing from her ears, and a sap-stained leather book sits beside her ledger.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: Sharp eyes, sweetheart, though staring does not buy a drink. An innkeeper has to keep track of every debt owed in this hollow, old ones included.
new: Staring does not buy a drink, sweetheart. An innkeeper must track every debt in this hollow, old ones included.

speaker: Narrator
old: The village is all shutters and held breath. In the middle of the trodden square an oak stands bare and gnarled, its bark carved with a hundred faces, and a bound shape is staked in the dirt beside it.
new: The square is all shutters and held breath. Beside a bare oak carved with a hundred faces, a bound shape is staked in the dirt.

speaker: Narrator
old: In the dark it could be anyone, bound and still, and the wolves are coming too fast for a long look.
new: In the dark it could be anyone, and the wolves are coming too fast for a long look.

speaker: Narrator
old: {name} slits the sacking with a quick stroke. A baby goat tumbles out, bleats once like an insult, and bolts across the square.
new: {name} slits the sacking. A baby goat tumbles out, bleats like an insult, and bolts across the square.

speaker: Narrator
old: {name} slits the doll and takes the goat in both arms before it finds its feet. It bleats against your collar, warm and furious.
new: {name} slits the doll and catches the goat in both arms. It bleats against your collar, warm and furious.

speaker: Narrator
old: You keep back and let the wolves come. They pour into the square, take the bound shape in a roil of fur and teeth, and are gone down the east road, and the square is quiet again.
new: You hold back as the wolves take the bound shape in a roil of fur and teeth, then vanish down the east road.

speaker: Narrator
old: You stand with hands loose and watch the wolves take the bound shape in a roil of fur and teeth. The pack leaves as it came, down the east road, and nothing in the whole village stirs.
new: You stand idle as the wolves take the bound shape and leave down the east road. Nothing in the village stirs.

speaker: Narrator
old: The wolves come down the east road in a shaggy wave, yellow eyes on the little white shape, and they do not care who is in the way.
new: The wolves pour down the east road, yellow eyes on the little white shape, caring nothing for who stands in the way.

speaker: morgan
old: Half the square is abed since the picnic, burning with fever and coughing up bitter rind. The sickness sits right inside the fruit, and my draughts only slow it.
new: Half the square is abed since the picnic, feverish and coughing up bitter rind. The sickness is in the fruit, and my draughts only slow it.

speaker: morgan
old: Folks are withering like frost-bitten clover, dry in the throat and hollow in the eye. If the root of it is not cut before long, the frail ones will not rise.
new: Folks are withering like frost-bitten clover. If the root is not cut soon, the frail ones will not rise.

speaker: morgan
old: Cecil Marl brought four barrels down from his orchard, along with comb honey and sweet cream. His trees were barren all last year, yet now they groan with red fruit.
new: Cecil Marl brought four barrels from his orchard, with comb honey and sweet cream. Barren all last year, his trees now groan with red fruit.

speaker: morgan
old: Follow the east lane past the hedgerows until you smell overripe cider and sulfur. Watch yourselves in his house, for no honest harvest turns the core to ash.
new: Follow the east lane past the hedgerows toward the smell of overripe cider and sulfur. Watch yourselves in his house; no honest harvest turns the core to ash.

speaker: Narrator
old: Sweat gleams on Cecil's cheeks despite the chill, and something small and leathery scratches inside the wainscoting.
new: Sweat gleams on Cecil's cold cheeks, and something small and leathery scratches inside the wainscoting.

speaker: cecil_marl
old: Come in, friends, come in out of the damp and try a dipper of sweet press! A man cannot help it if his boughs are blessed while the moor goes hungry.
new: Come in out of the damp, friends, and try a dipper of sweet press! I cannot help it if my boughs are blessed while the moor goes hungry.

speaker: cecil_marl
old: Wait now, I only signed for golden boughs and a full cellar, I never asked who paid the price! Stay back, or my little helpers will peel you to the bone!
new: I only signed for golden boughs and a full cellar, I never asked who paid! Stay back, or my little helpers will peel you to the bone!

speaker: cecil_marl
old: Sickness? Why, village bellies are just too weak for proper rich cream and cellar cider, that is all it is.
new: Sickness? Village bellies are just too weak for rich cream and cellar cider.

speaker: Narrator
old: Outside, the heavy red apples shrivel to gray ash on the boughs, and the sour heat in the air breaks like a fever.
new: Outside, the red apples shrivel to gray ash on the boughs, and the sour heat breaks like a fever.

speaker: morgan
old: The village is breathing easy again, and the children are already asking for broth. Whatever foul bargain fed those roots has gone back to the pit with its master.
new: The village breathes easy again, and the children are asking for broth. Whatever foul bargain fed those roots has gone back to the pit with its master.

speaker: Narrator
old: Sweet pipe smoke and oiled leather hang warm in the rafters of the post. Behind the counter, a slender man in spotless grey studies you with dark, practiced eyes.
new: Pipe smoke and oiled leather warm the rafters. Behind the counter, a slender man in spotless grey studies you.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: Step in out of the damp, friends. If it exists in Druskenvald, it passes through Tolliver's Trading Post sooner or later, and if it does not, I know who carries it.
new: Step in, friends. Everything in Druskenvald passes through Tolliver's Trading Post sooner or later, or I know who carries it.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: A man goes where he is needed, and the moor had a sharp need for civilised commerce. Besides, the air out here has been waking up lately.
new: The moor had a sharp need for civilised commerce. Besides, the air out here has been waking up lately.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: Mayor Somerton keeps his flock singing to oaks and stones, and they pay their bills on time. Keep your blades sheathed indoors and we will get along splendidly.
new: Mayor Somerton keeps his flock singing to oaks and stones, and they pay on time. Keep your blades sheathed indoors and we will get along.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: If you fancy odd machinery, there is a riverboat engine down on the water built by another Stranger like yourselves. Folks pay good coin for parts from the old world.
new: Down on the water sits a riverboat engine built by another Stranger like yourselves. Folks pay good coin for old-world parts.

speaker: Narrator
old: Where his silver ring taps the mahogany bowl, a leaping hare is worked into the dark grain, and tiny antlers are stamped inside the band.
new: A leaping hare is worked into his mahogany pipe bowl, and tiny antlers are stamped inside his silver ring.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: You have a sharp eye for small work. An old family token from the deep woods, nothing I keep on the shelves for sale.
new: Sharp eye. An old family token from the deep woods, not for sale.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: Careful staring too long at a merchant's hands, friend, or I will think you are pricing my rings.
new: Stare too long at a merchant's hands, friend, and I will think you are pricing my rings.

speaker: Narrator
old: The smell of fresh pine shavings and warm linseed oil spills from the open workshop. Beatrice planes a curved beam in time to a bright, three-part tune hummed from the rafters.
new: Pine shavings and warm linseed oil scent the open workshop. Beatrice planes a curved beam to a three-part tune hummed from the rafters.

speaker: beatrice_wells
old: Branden turns the lathe, the four little ones sweep and fetch the pegs, and I shape the frames. A workshop that sings together never splits the grain.
new: Branden turns the lathe, the four little ones sweep and fetch pegs, and I shape the frames. A workshop that sings together never splits the grain.

speaker: beatrice_wells
old: Brother Weston asked us to raise the new Brightsinger chapel with high, clear eaves. Half the Old Ways folk mutter as they pass, but good oak answers to any honest chisel.
new: Brother Weston asked for high, clear eaves on the new Brightsinger chapel. Old Ways folk mutter, but good oak answers to any honest chisel.

speaker: beatrice_wells
old: Look up at that old house on the hill when the moon catches the roof. Not a single rafter sits square, yet the whole pitch leans together without a creak.
new: Look at that old house on the hill in the moonlight. Not a rafter sits square, yet the whole pitch leans together without a creak.

speaker: Narrator
old: Beneath the chapel plans lie dozens of frantic charcoal drawings, each repeating the same impossible, crooked dovetail joint.
new: Beneath the chapel plans lie dozens of frantic charcoal sketches of the same impossible, crooked dovetail joint.

speaker: beatrice_wells
old: Look at that angle, it ought to collapse under its own weight, yet it holds like iron. If I could just puzzle out how the builder bent the king-post, my chapel spire would touch the stars.
new: That angle ought to collapse, yet it holds like iron. If I could puzzle out how the builder bent the king-post, my chapel spire would touch the stars.

speaker: beatrice_wells
old: Only timber tallies and choir sheets under there, friend, nothing half so grand as the finished roof will be.
new: Only timber tallies and choir sheets under there, friend, nothing so grand as the finished roof.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: The new bronze bell sits on a handcart down by the south footbridge, and my back has given out. The ruts are deep, and the clocktower has stood dumb for a week.
new: The new bronze bell is stuck in deep ruts by the south footbridge, and my back gave out. The clocktower has stood dumb for a week.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: The old bell split clean down the seam the night the Oak last stirred. Folk lose count of the six hours without a chime to steady them.
new: The old bell split down the seam the night the Oak last stirred. Folk lose count of the six hours without a chime.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: Bless your strong shoulders. Bring the cart round to the belfry steps before the dusk mist thickens, and mind the axle in the mud.
new: Bless your strong shoulders. Bring the cart to the belfry steps before the dusk mist thickens, and mind the axle in the mud.

speaker: Narrator
old: The heavy bronze bell rests under damp straw on a creaking timber cart. Before you can lift the shafts, a whiskered man in a faded coat marches up.
new: The heavy bronze bell rests under damp straw on a creaking timber cart. As you reach for the shafts, a whiskered man in a faded coat marches up.

speaker: sgt_gaunt
old: Halt and take heart, travellers. At Pipers Ford I held a baggage train against forty bandits, three steps from a stand, and I shall guard this bell myself.
new: Halt, travellers. I held a train against forty bandits at Pipers Ford, three steps from a stand, and I shall guard this bell myself.

speaker: Narrator
old: A rook croaks sharply from the bridge rail, and the sergeant drops flat beneath the cart axle, clutching his hat.
new: A rook croaks from the bridge rail, and the sergeant drops flat under the axle, clutching his hat.

speaker: Narrator
old: The narrow cobbles of the market lane teem with barrows, geese, and crooked lanterns. One iron-shod wheel drops into a gutter, tilting the great bronze bell toward a stone wall.
new: Barrows, geese, and crooked lanterns crowd the market lane. A wheel drops into a gutter, tilting the bronze bell toward a stone wall.

speaker: Narrator
old: {name} braces a shoulder against the timber side and heaves the cart level before the bronze can kiss the wall.
new: {name} braces a shoulder against the timber and heaves the cart level before the bronze kisses the wall.

speaker: Narrator
old: The cart lurches and the bronze rim strikes the masonry with a dull, sour ring, leaving a hairline crack across its lip.
new: The cart lurches and the bronze rim strikes the stone with a sour ring, cracking its lip.

speaker: Narrator
old: The outer moor road winds through black peat and ankle-deep mire, where sunken stones wait to snap an axle.
new: The outer moor road winds through black peat and mire, where sunken stones wait to snap an axle.

speaker: Narrator
old: {name} reads the tufts of dry heather and guides the wheels along a ridge of buried gravel.
new: {name} reads the dry heather and guides the wheels along a ridge of buried gravel.

speaker: Narrator
old: The wheels sink twice into the wet peat, and the last grey sheen of dusk is fading by the time you haul the cart free.
new: The wheels sink twice into wet peat, and dusk is fading by the time you haul the cart free.

speaker: Narrator
old: The straw beside the bell rustles, and a small boy pokes his head out, his pockets clinking with loose buttons.
new: The straw rustles, and a small boy pokes his head out, pockets clinking with loose buttons.

speaker: Narrator
old: {name} spots horn and pewter buttons dropped every ten paces down the rutted track, with Pip's mother already marching up the lane following them.
new: {name} spots horn and pewter buttons dropped every ten paces down the track, with Pip's mother already marching up behind them.

speaker: pip_oakum
old: Botheration, the pocket with the hole in it! Do not let her take my tin military ones!
new: Botheration, the pocket with the hole! Do not let her take my tin military ones!

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: Here she is, safe at the belfry steps. Lend a hand on the hoist rope and hear her speak.
new: Safe at the belfry steps. Lend a hand on the hoist rope and hear her speak.

speaker: Narrator
old: The new bell swings into the dark timber tower and tolls a single, deep note that rolls out over the Round.
new: The new bell swings into the dark timber tower and tolls a single, deep note over the Round.

speaker: Narrator
old: You leave the cart by the footbridge, and by the time a hired labourer drags it to the Round, Solomon's face is set like gravestone.
new: You leave the cart by the footbridge. By the time a hired labourer drags it to the Round, Solomon's face is set like gravestone.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: A mason keeps his word when he takes a job, stranger. Remember that next time you offer your hands.
new: A mason keeps his word, stranger. Remember that next time you offer your hands.

speaker: Narrator
old: Cedar curls cling to Branden's bright waistcoat as he taps a wooden peg home, humming a warm bass harmony beneath his wife's soprano.
new: Cedar curls cling to Branden's bright waistcoat as he taps a peg home, humming a bass harmony beneath his wife's soprano.

speaker: branden_wells
old: Evening to you, travellers! Always room by the workbench for another pair of ears, long as you don't mind a bit of sawdust in your hair.
new: Evening, travellers! Always room by the workbench, long as you don't mind sawdust in your hair.

speaker: branden_wells
old: Robin and Lark sort the dowels, Jay minds the glue, and little Wren mostly steals the shavings for curls. Give me a tight roof, a full supper pot, and four beds tucked in, and I'm a rich man.
new: Robin and Lark sort dowels, Jay minds the glue, and little Wren steals shavings for curls. With a tight roof, a full pot, and four beds tucked in, I'm a rich man.

speaker: branden_wells
old: Wickermoor's a dark pitch for raising little birds, I won't lie. Still, the neighbours buy our wagons, and Mayor Somerton respects a straight wheel even if we sing with the Brightsingers.
new: Wickermoor's a dark pitch for raising little birds. Still, neighbours buy our wagons, and Mayor Somerton respects a straight wheel even if we sing with the Brightsingers.

speaker: branden_wells
old: The quarry men brought down a load of ridge timber last week with hare tracks carved deep in the bark. I burned those planks in the stove rather than plane them.
new: Quarry men brought down ridge timber last week with hare tracks carved deep in the bark. I burned those planks in the stove rather than plane them.

speaker: Narrator
old: His thumb smooths a toy songbird carved from scrap pine, and the cheerful crinkle around his eyes fades as he glances toward the hill.
new: His thumb smooths a pine songbird, and the crinkle around his eyes fades as he glances toward the hill.

speaker: branden_wells
old: Bea stands at the window half the night measuring that crooked roof on the ridge with her callipers. I just want the chapel roofed and our shutters barred before whatever lives up there notices her looking.
new: Bea stands at the window half the night measuring that crooked roof on the ridge with her callipers. I want the chapel roofed and our shutters barred before whatever lives up there notices.

speaker: branden_wells
old: Only a dry throat from singing counter-part since the third chime, friend, nothing a mug of cider won't mend.
new: Only a dry throat from singing counter-part since the third chime, friend. Nothing a mug of cider won't mend.

speaker: rose_somerton
old: Father says we must keep our boots wiped and welcome the grand folk properly. You have mud on yours, just like the men he feeds to the big tree.
new: Father says to keep our boots wiped and welcome grand folk properly. You have mud on yours, like the men he feeds to the big tree.

speaker: rose_somerton
old: Mother told me to hush my mouth about the roots drinking red, or the hare with the horns will scratch at my shutter.
new: Mother told me to hush about the roots drinking red, or the horned hare will scratch at my shutter.

speaker: rose_somerton
old: He says the Green Queen watches every hearth, and anyone who locks their door at night has something rotten in the cellar.
new: He says the Green Queen watches every hearth, and anyone locking their door at night hides something rotten in the cellar.

speaker: victoria_wainwright
old: Stand clear of the crates, if you please. I am minding Eddie and Zachariah while the Trading Post is busy, and I do not know your faces.
new: Stand clear of the crates, please. I am minding Eddie and Zachariah while the Trading Post is busy, and I do not know your faces.

speaker: victoria_wainwright
old: Since the fog took our mother and father out by Dawn's Gate. Folks here give us broth and blankets, though they never look toward the road.
new: Since the fog took our mother and father by Dawn's Gate. Folks give us broth and blankets, though they never look toward the road.

speaker: victoria_wainwright
old: Eddie trades buttons to keep his hands busy, and little Zachariah has hardly spoken since Foxwillow burned. I watch the latches after dark for both of them.
new: Eddie trades buttons to keep his hands busy, and Zachariah has hardly spoken since Foxwillow burned. I watch the latches after dark.

speaker: victoria_wainwright
old: Keep your lantern trimmed if you walk past the square. The dark comes down thick around the eaves.
new: Keep your lantern trimmed past the square. The dark comes down thick around the eaves.

speaker: eddie_wainwright
old: Four tin caps for a brass button, or two horn buttons for a buckle. That is my price, strangers, take it or walk on.
new: Four tin caps for a brass button, or two horn buttons for a buckle. Take it or walk on, strangers.

speaker: eddie_wainwright
old: Down in the ditch behind the Oak, mostly. Folk drop all sorts of good brass when the headsman is done with them.
new: Down in the ditch behind the Oak, mostly. Folk drop good brass when the headsman is done with them.

speaker: eddie_wainwright
old: Wet boots and cold eels, that is all Murkwater ever was. Here the mud is drier, even if the moon stares harder.
new: Wet boots and cold eels, that was Murkwater. Here the mud is drier, even if the moon stares harder.

speaker: eddie_wainwright
old: Hold on to your coat buttons then. I will find them in the weeds sooner or later.
new: Keep your coat buttons then. I will find them in the weeds sooner or later.

speaker: zachariah_wainwright
old: Do not step on the charcoal, please. If you smudge the pumpkin man's feet, he cannot stay on the stone.
new: Do not step on the charcoal, please. Smudge the pumpkin man's feet and he cannot stay on the stone.

speaker: zachariah_wainwright
old: He stands in the furrows and keeps the crows inside his coat. You have to draw his grin wide so he does not get hungry.
new: He stands in the furrows keeping crows inside his coat. Draw his grin wide so he does not get hungry.

speaker: zachariah_wainwright
old: The thatch all turned to orange sparks, and the straw men walked out of the field by themselves. Victoria says I only dreamed it.
new: The thatch turned to orange sparks, and the straw men walked out of the field. Victoria says I only dreamed it.

speaker: Narrator
old: The boy taps a piece of burnt twig against the cobbles, giving the sketched scarecrow a third crooked eye.
new: The boy taps a burnt twig against the cobbles, giving the sketched scarecrow a third crooked eye.

speaker: sofia_roderick
old: Here lies Thomas, cold as clay, borrowed a spade and stayed all day. I sweep the stone dust for Father and make up verses for the blank slabs.
new: Here lies Thomas, cold as clay, borrowed a spade and stayed all day. I sweep stone dust for Father and make up verses for blank slabs.

speaker: sofia_roderick
old: Father only cuts names and dates, nice and square. He says folk in Wickermoor want a heavy stone over them so nothing digs them up.
new: Father only cuts names and dates, nice and square. Folk in Wickermoor want a heavy stone over them so nothing digs them up.

speaker: sofia_roderick
old: My mother taught me before she walked out past the boundary stones with her shawl packed. Father says she went to look for morning.
new: Mother taught me before she walked past the boundary stones with her shawl packed. Father says she went to look for morning.

speaker: robin_wells
old: One for sorrow, two for mirth, three for a wedding, four for a birth. There are four of you walking together, and the clock has only struck once.
new: One for sorrow, two for mirth, three for a wedding, four for a birth. Four of you walk together, and the clock has only struck once.

speaker: robin_wells
old: Four birds in a newly woven basket, brought up to the manor gate. Mind the cat does not unlatch the wicker.
new: Four birds in a new basket, brought to the manor gate. Mind the cat does not unlatch the wicker.

speaker: lark_wells
old: Hold still and let me listen to your boots. Every soul in Wickermoor has a bird in their chest, if you have the ear for it.
new: Hold still and let me listen to your boots. Every soul in Wickermoor has a bird in their chest, if you have the ear.

speaker: lark_wells
old: Rook and starling and chimney swift,blown in under a storm cloud. You have not learned the local call yet.
new: Rook, starling, and chimney swift, blown in under a storm cloud. You have not learned the local call yet.

speaker: jay_wells
old: Bet you a copper you cannot whistle loud enough to bounce off the clocktower bell. Watch me do it with two fingers.
new: Bet a copper you cannot whistle loud enough to bounce off the clocktower bell. Watch me do it with two fingers.

speaker: jay_wells
old: If you hit the note right before the hour strikes, the bats come pouring out of the belfry like black soot.
new: Hit the note right before the hour strikes, and bats pour out of the belfry like black soot.

speaker: jay_wells
old: Mother says a loud boy is a boy the moor-hounds will not bother chewing. They prefer the quiet ones who creep along the wall.
new: Mother says moor-hounds will not bother chewing a loud boy. They prefer quiet ones creeping along the wall.

speaker: jay_wells
old: Go on then, keep your copper. Your ears are too stiff for a proper country whistle anyway.
new: Keep your copper then. Your ears are too stiff for a proper country whistle.

speaker: wren_wells
old: Robin told me to stay on the porch step until the hymn is finished. You have very long shadows.
new: Robin told me to stay on the porch step until the hymn finishes. You have very long shadows.

speaker: wren_wells
old: The faces in the oak tree look different when strangers walk by. One of them opened its mouth when you crossed the Round.
new: The faces in the oak look different when strangers pass. One opened its mouth when you crossed the Round.

speaker: violet_aster
old: Twelve loaves on the cooling rack, seven candles in the window, three sacks of rye by the trough. You have to count everything twice before Mother's birthday.
new: Twelve loaves, seven candles, three sacks of rye. You have to count everything twice before Mother's birthday.

speaker: violet_aster
old: When the count comes up short, something has been in the pantry. Yesterday there were four hare tracks in the spilled flour.
new: When the count comes up short, something's been in the pantry. Yesterday there were four hare tracks in the spilled flour.

speaker: violet_aster
old: Mother smiles and braids sunflower stalks into the dough, but Father sits by the cold oven after closing and wipes his eyes with his apron.
new: Mother smiles and braids sunflower stalks into the dough, while Father sits by the cold oven wiping his eyes.

speaker: lavender_aster
old: Here, take a crust of honey-twist while it is still warm from the peel. Everything tastes sweeter before the third bell.
new: Take a crust of honey-twist while it is warm from the peel. Everything tastes sweeter before the third bell.

speaker: lavender_aster
old: Mother puts caraway and dried marigold in the glaze for the Patient Lady. It keeps the damp out of your ribs.
new: Mother glazes them with caraway and dried marigold for the Patient Lady. Keeps the damp out of your ribs.

speaker: lavender_aster
old: We are baking three tiers of spiced cake for Mother's birthday. Everyone in the square is invited, even the glum folk.
new: We are baking a three-tier spiced cake for Mother's birthday. The whole square is invited, even the glum folk.

speaker: lavender_aster
old: Violet tallies the flour bins until her fingers ache. I tell her the mice take a pinch for their supper and she ought to let them.
new: Violet tallies the flour bins until her fingers ache. I tell her to let the mice have their pinch.

speaker: ulf_harga
old: Good health to you, tall folk. Do not slam the pen gate, or Old Bristle-Back will think the cleaver is coming for him before his day.
new: Good health, tall folk. Do not slam the pen gate, or Old Bristle-Back will think the cleaver is coming.

speaker: ulf_harga
old: Every swine has a true name. That spotted sow is Freydis, and the black boar is Kettle-Snout; a named beast gives honest meat.
new: That spotted sow is Freydis, and the black boar is Kettle-Snout. A named beast gives honest meat.

speaker: ulf_harga
old: My brother keeps the long knives bright as ice. He says we feed the village body and bone, and we waste not a drop of blood.
new: My brother keeps the long knives bright as ice. We feed the village and waste not a drop of blood.

speaker: ulf_harga
old: Walk hale, strangers. If you have turnip peelings in your packs, Kettle-Snout will remember you kindly.
new: Walk hale, strangers. Kettle-Snout will remember you kindly if you have turnip peelings.

speaker: peter_murdoch
old: Have you washed your hands and given your names to the choir, strangers? Father says the night here only ends for those who learn the canticle.
new: Have you washed your hands and given the choir your names? Father says night here only ends once you learn the canticle.

speaker: peter_murdoch
old: We came to hang brass lanterns where these country folk hang dry bones. One clear voice can scatter a hundred owls.
new: We came to hang brass lanterns where these folk hang dry bones. One clear voice scatters a hundred owls.

speaker: peter_murdoch
old: They bow to an ugly root-split tree and whisper to hares in the grass. It is heathen muck, every bit of it.
new: They bow to a root-split tree and whisper to hares. Heathen muck, all of it.

speaker: peter_murdoch
old: Come to the chapel bench when the bell tolls. You look as though you need the dust sung off your coats.
new: Come to the chapel when the bell tolls. You need the dust sung off your coats.

speaker: charlotte_murdoch
old: Never mind Peter, he swallows Father's sermons whole like a gull with a herring. Do you know any tavern catches from the city?
new: Never mind Peter, he swallows Father's sermons like a gull with a herring. Know any city tavern catches?

speaker: charlotte_murdoch
old: If I hear one more verse about dawn breaking over the hills, I shall scream. Look up at that moon; she is not going anywhere.
new: One more verse about dawn breaking and I shall scream. Look at that moon; she is not going anywhere.

speaker: charlotte_murdoch
old: The Brightsingers have pretty tunes, and the Old Ways have big bonfires, and neither one keeps the roof from leaking when the moor rain starts.
new: The Brightsingers have tunes and the Old Ways have bonfires, and neither stops the roof leaking in the moor rain.

speaker: margery_heyling
old: Wipe your soles on the sacking before you come near the shelves, please. My aunt has a headachy spell, and I have three ledgers left to ink.
new: Wipe your soles before approaching the shelves. My aunt has a headache, and I have three ledgers to ink.

speaker: margery_heyling
old: Since Mother died, someone has to see that the kettle boils and the folios stay dry. Auntie means well, but her mind wanders into the stacks.
new: Since Mother died, I keep the kettle boiling and the folios dry. Auntie's mind wanders into the stacks.

speaker: margery_heyling
old: Algernon reads until the tallow gutters out, and Sheridan hides under the counter stealing peppermint drops. They are a full day's work by themselves.
new: Algernon reads until the tallow gutters, and Sheridan hides under the counter stealing peppermint drops.

speaker: margery_heyling
old: Do not pull a volume from the bottom row unless you mean to buy it. The bindings are older than the square.
new: Do not pull a bottom-row volume unless you mean to buy. Those bindings are older than the square.

speaker: algernon_heyling
old: Did you know a moorland hare can sleep with both eyes open, and an oak tree drinks forty gallons of water a day, or blood if the soil is sour?
new: Did you know moorland hares sleep with both eyes open, and oaks drink forty gallons of water a day, or blood in sour soil?

speaker: algernon_heyling
old: In the green-bound herbal on the third shelf up. Auntie says it is for grown scholars, which only means she keeps it behind the step-stool.
new: In the green herbal on the third shelf. Auntie says it is for scholars and hides it behind the step-stool.

speaker: algernon_heyling
old: The village charter has seven signatures at the bottom, but the founder's name was scraped off the parchment with a razor. You can still feel the rough spot.
new: The village charter has seven signatures, but the founder's name was razor-scraped off. You can feel the rough spot.

speaker: sheridan_heyling
old: I can see your ankles from under the tablecloth. Have you got any barley sugar or candied peel in your pockets?
new: I see your ankles from under the tablecloth. Got any barley sugar or candied peel?

speaker: sheridan_heyling
old: Bless your boots! Do not tell Margery, or she will make me wash the inkpots before I can suck it down.
new: Bless your boots! Do not tell Margery, or she will make me wash the inkpots first.

speaker: sheridan_heyling
old: People look at your face when you sit on a chair, and sometimes a face in the window looks back. Down here it is only dust and shoe-buckles.
new: Sit on a chair and sometimes a face in the window looks back. Down here is only dust and shoe-buckles.

speaker: sheridan_heyling
old: All those buckles and pouches and not one lemon drop. You are very poor travellers.
new: All those buckles and pouches and not one lemon drop. Poor travellers you are.

speaker: dani_jenkin
old: Easy, Shuck, keep your teeth to yourself. You four do not need to crowd the path; the wet woman walking behind your left shoulder wants room too.
new: Easy, Shuck. Do not crowd the path, you four; the wet woman behind your left shoulder wants room too.

speaker: dani_jenkin
old: Only a drowned girl with river-weed in her hem, staring at your lantern. They follow newly arrived folk until they remember they have nowhere to go.
new: A drowned girl with river-weed in her hem, staring at your lantern. They follow newcomers until they remember they have nowhere to go.

speaker: dani_jenkin
old: Shuck has been with me since I could toddle. He growls at the bad dead and puts his chin on my knee when the harmless ones chatter.
new: Shuck growls at the bad dead and rests his chin on my knee when the harmless ones chatter.

speaker: dani_jenkin
old: Keep moving toward the firelight. The ones without faces do not like the smell of burning birch.
new: Keep toward the firelight. The faceless ones hate the smell of burning birch.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
old: I know the pull of a tight seam along the ribs, and the thread has to give when you breathe.
new: I know the pull of a tight rib seam; the thread must give when you breathe.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
old: Try this charcoal silk on, I lined the ruby-glass buttonholes to cushion your vials.
new: Try this charcoal silk. I lined the ruby-glass buttonholes to cushion your vials.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
old: Glass leaves a jagged line when it goes in, and the needle leaves a straight one coming out.
new: Glass leaves a jagged line going in; the needle leaves a straight one coming out.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: Welcome to the Green Queen, my dears, though I see your table will require an extra place setting.
new: Welcome to the Green Queen, my dears, though your table will need an extra place setting.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: Forgive the liberty, my dear, but a gentleman's invisible lapel should lie flat when he visits my house.
new: Forgive the liberty, my dear, but a gentleman's invisible lapel should lie flat in my house.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: Such lively company rarely lingers without a heavy ledger, so let me offer a house blessing for the story of how you met.
new: Such lively company carries a heavy ledger; let me offer a house blessing for the story of how you met.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: Sensible friends are worth their weight in silver, and a good story pours better than vintage wine.
new: Sensible friends are worth silver, and a good story pours better than vintage wine.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: I admire fine needlework wherever it walks in, and Picco felt is so rarely seen this far out.
new: I admire fine needlework, and Picco felt is rarely seen this far out.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: Every sturdy seam has its provenance, and I always pay fair market value for a rarity.
new: Every sturdy seam has its provenance, and I pay fair market value for a rarity.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: May the Green Queen keep your threads dry and your patron polite while you rest under my roof.
new: May the Green Queen keep your threads dry and your patron polite under my roof.

speaker: alda_farnum
old: When you are ready to settle the rest of the account, you know right where the counter is.
new: When you are ready to settle the account, you know where the counter is.

speaker: hilda_brom
old: Catch this pine-sprig. Smear the crow-grease on your cuffs. Look south-east to Foxwillow corn, where something worse than a fugitive stalks the rows.
new: Catch this pine-sprig and smear crow-grease on your cuffs. Something worse than a fugitive stalks the Foxwillow corn south-east.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Warden, by the cut of the leather and the chalk under your nails. I have set out grey grave-wax and a stick of mason's chalk on the trestle.
new: A Warden, by your leather and the chalk under your nails. Grey grave-wax and mason's chalk are on the trestle.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Your ledger is kept to a clean standard, Warden, dry edges and honest dates, the way Yorgrim kept Maidenmist Cemetery before he went quiet.
new: Your ledger is clean and honest, Warden, the way Yorgrim kept Maidenmist Cemetery before he went quiet.

speaker: mori_shade
old: I have marked one cross at the soured fields of Foxwillow, where the drainage fails and the dead lie uneasy. The other sites will show themselves to a working eye.
new: I marked one cross at Foxwillow's soured fields, where the dead lie uneasy. A working eye will find the other sites.

speaker: mori_shade
old: There is only one trade when the candles burn down, stranger. We keep the boundary between those who walk and those who rest.
new: One trade remains when the candles burn down, stranger: keeping the boundary between those who walk and those who rest.

speaker: mori_shade
old: What counts in this valley is the hand that holds the shovel, and what the pin is fastened to.
new: What counts here is the hand on the shovel, and what the pin is fastened to.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Walk with a measured step on the Foxwillow clay, for the turf is thin over the old pits.
new: Step carefully on the Foxwillow clay; the turf is thin over the old pits.

speaker: mori_shade
old: May the earth lie level under your boots, Warden, and may your own bones keep the cold that steadies them.
new: May the earth lie level under your boots, Warden, and your bones keep their steadying cold.

speaker: holly_aster
old: Take this loaf while the crust is still singing, before Violet and Lavender turn my cooling racks into a fort.
new: Take this loaf while the crust sings, before Violet and Lavender turn my cooling racks into a fort.

speaker: holly_aster
old: Don't mind your little shadow tapping at my wrist, it's only a grey spade-mark I've carried since the cradle.
new: Mind not your shadow tapping my wrist; I've carried this grey spade-mark since the cradle.

speaker: holly_aster
old: An unseen creditor holds the deed to my thirty-fifth birthday, and the only ledger office floats on that neon riverboat at the Drowned Crossroads.
new: An unseen creditor holds the deed to my thirty-fifth birthday, with a ledger office on that neon riverboat at the Drowned Crossroads.

speaker: holly_aster
old: Keep your voice down over the oven's roar, or my girls will think we're telling ghost stories before supper.
new: Keep your voice down over the oven, or my girls will think we're telling ghost stories.

speaker: holly_aster
old: Every woman in my line gets thirty-five bright years to bake the bread and raise the girls, and then the tab comes due.
new: Women in my line get thirty-five years to bake bread and raise girls before the tab comes due.

speaker: holly_aster
old: That's sensible talk, because a warm rye loaf is a much safer thing to carry than a baker's bad luck.
new: Sensible talk; a warm rye loaf is safer to carry than a baker's bad luck.

speaker: holly_aster
old: Hold out your palm and take this pinch of blessed hearth-salt, the Old Ways say it keeps a creditor's ink from drying.
new: Take this pinch of blessed hearth-salt; the Old Ways say it keeps a creditor's ink wet.

speaker: holly_aster
old: Now eat that crust before it cools, or I'll charge you double just for standing in my flour.
new: Eat that crust before it cools, or I'll charge double for standing in my flour.

speaker: sister_rain
old: The Patient Lady says we tend what grows and bind what splits, and we never answer blight with a torch.
new: The Patient Lady says to tend what grows, bind what splits, and never answer blight with a torch.

speaker: sister_rain
old: Bite your tongue, the land is bleeding enough without you calling down iron and fire on it!
new: Bite your tongue! The land bleeds enough without you calling down iron and fire!

speaker: sister_rain
old: Listen to me roaring like a March gale when your friend here just saved my best pumpkin.
new: Listen to me roaring like a March gale after your friend saved my best pumpkin.

speaker: sister_rain
old: When you have the stomach for worse than a bruised vine, the sick places round the village are crying out for a steady hand.
new: When you have the stomach for worse than a bruised vine, the village's sick places need a steady hand.

speaker: morgan
old: Hold a moment, friend. You have got that same blank look in your eyes that I see in the water bucket every morning.
new: Hold on, friend. You have the same blank look I see in my water bucket every morning.

speaker: Narrator
old: A scrap offolded paper rustles between {name}'s fingers, smelling faintly of damp wool and pressed lavender.
new: A folded paper scrap rustles between {name}'s fingers, smelling of damp wool and pressed lavender.

speaker: morgan
old: Like you woke up in the heather with your pockets empty and your own name feeling like a borrowed coat.
new: Like you woke in the heather with empty pockets and your name feeling like a borrowed coat.

speaker: morgan
old: Wait. Da-dum, then the drop into the minor? Saints above, I have whistled that second half while sweeping the hearth for three winters.
new: Da-dum, then the minor drop? Saints above, I have whistled that second half by the hearth for three winters.

speaker: morgan
old: Two years come the next tolling, give or take. Folks here are kind enough, provided you pull your weight and do not ask where the road leads.
new: Two years next tolling. Folks here are kind if you pull your weight and never ask where the road leads.

speaker: morgan
old: Fair enough, I will not pry. When you have nothing in your head but mist, even the mist feels like private property.
new: I will not pry. When your head holds only mist, even mist feels like private property.

speaker: morgan
old: Take a look at this handbill I found tucked in a crate of salt. It speaks of a house called Memory's Rest, out where the forgetful go to sit.
new: Look at this handbill from a salt crate. It speaks of Memory's Rest, a house where the forgetful sit.

speaker: morgan
old: Keep your ears open for the rest of that tune, friend. If you find out who we were, save a verse for me.
new: Keep listening for the rest of that tune, friend. If you learn who we were, save me a verse.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: Pardon the intrusion, traveler, but my nose rarely deceives me. That is coal smoke, cold iron, and river fog clinging to your hem.
new: Pardon, traveler, but I smell coal smoke, cold iron, and river fog on your hem.

speaker: Narrator
old: He tips his hat with a gloved hand, and the faint chime of a brass ticket punch clicks inside his waistcoat pocket.
new: He tips his hat with a gloved hand, a brass ticket punch chiming in his waistcoat pocket.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: Only one engine in all of Druskenvald burns fuel like that. You have ridden the Ghostlight Express before tonight, have you not?
new: Only one engine in Druskenvald burns that fuel. You have ridden the Ghostlight Express before tonight, yes?

speaker: Player
old: I know the sound of those wheels on the trestle. Once you hear it, ordinary iron sounds dead.
new: I know those wheels on the trestle. After that, ordinary iron sounds dead.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: Quite so, quite so. A passenger of distinction never truly steps off the platform, no matter how far inland they wander.
new: Quite so. A passenger of distinction never truly leaves the platform, however far inland they wander.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: A man of commerce must watch the timetables, my dear friend. Freight moves by rail, by cart, and by darker conveyances when the moon allows.
new: A merchant watches the timetables, friend. Freight moves by rail, cart, and darker conveyances when the moon allows.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: Of course, my mistake entirely. The moorland damp plays curious tricks on velvet and wool alike.
new: My mistake entirely. The moorland damp plays curious tricks on velvet and wool.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: Still, should you ever long for that particular furnace heat again, look downriver. The Stranger keeps another engine churning inside a paddlewheel hull.
new: Should you long for that furnace heat again, look downriver. The Stranger keeps another engine churning inside a paddlewheel hull.

speaker: Narrator
old: The lantern light catches the rim of his spectacles, turning his eyes into two flat coins of yellow glass.
new: Lantern light catches his spectacles, turning his eyes into flat coins of yellow glass.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: Do call on my counter whenever your purse feels heavy. We understand one another, you and I, and I always favor repeat travelers.
new: Call on my counter when your purse is heavy. We understand one another, and I favor repeat travelers.

speaker: Narrator
old: The schoolmaster squints past {name}'s shoulder at the flagstones, where {name}'s shadow stretches a thumb's breadth too late to match the step.
new: The schoolmaster squints past {name} at the flagstones, where {name}'s shadow lags a thumb's breadth behind the step.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: Merciful heaven, there really are two of you. Or rather, there is you, and there is the piece of you that slipped its leash.
new: Merciful heaven, there are two of you: you, and the piece that slipped its leash.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: Three nights before the butcherings down by the sheepfold, someone with your exact stride passed my schoolhouse window. No lantern, no footfall on thefrost, heading north-east.
new: Three nights before the sheepfold butcherings, someone with your stride passed my schoolhouse heading north-east, without lantern or footfall on the frost.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: Scold me if you must, yet a man who teaches children to count knows when one and one make a wrong number.
new: Scold me if you must, but a counting teacher knows when one and one make a wrong number.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: I have kept notes on what the old monographs call the Grey. When a soul enters Druskenvald crookedly, the reflection and the meat divide at the threshold.
new: My notes on the old monographs call it the Grey: a soul entering Druskenvald crookedly divides meat from reflection at the threshold.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: Watch the puddles and the dark windowpanes, traveler. Whatever walked north-east toward the hills is already practicing your handwriting.
new: Watch the puddles and dark panes, traveler. Whatever walked north-east toward the hills is practicing your handwriting.

speaker: Narrator
old: Heat rolls off the forge behind him, carrying the sharp, coppery tang of quenched steel and old winter sweat.
new: Forge heat rolls off behind him, sharp with quenched steel and old winter sweat.

speaker: jean_myriel
old: I thought so. Only a Crimson aspirant holds a blade with the thumb high like a lancet, waiting for the vein to rise.
new: Only a Crimson aspirant holds a blade thumb-high like a lancet, waiting for the vein to rise.

speaker: Player
old: The ink faded when I crossed the mist, but the calluses stayed. We were taught that iron is thirsty until it drinks.
new: The ink faded in the mist, but the calluses stayed. We learned iron stays thirsty until it drinks.

speaker: jean_myriel
old: Aye, and the thirst never leaves the metal once you wake it. I folded my share of red steel before I laid the tongs down for good.
new: Aye, and waking the metal leaves it thirsty forever. I folded enough red steel before laying down the tongs.

speaker: jean_myriel
old: I wore the briar cord at my waist twenty years back. Tempered three swords in warm basins before I realized what the steel was taking from the smith.
new: I wore the briar cord twenty years back, tempering three swords in warm basins before seeing what the steel took from me.

speaker: jean_myriel
old: Keep your secrets if they warm you. An old anvil knows the hammer's weight whether the smith speaks or not.
new: Keep your secrets. An old anvil knows the hammer's weight whether the smith speaks or not.

speaker: jean_myriel
old: Hear me plain: if you go looking for the brothers at Dawn's Gate, turn your heels back to the valley. That monastery is a slaughterhouse dressed in stained glass.
new: If you seek the brothers at Dawn's Gate, turn back to the valley. That monastery is a slaughterhouse in stained glass.

speaker: jean_myriel
old: Here in Wickermoor, I mend plowshares and horse shoes, and nobody bleeds for a hinge. Come by the forge if you want honest iron.
new: In Wickermoor, I mend plowshares and horseshoes, and nobody bleeds for a hinge. Come by for honest iron.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: Keep your hands where the torchlight can find them, stranger. You walk with your shoulders crooked, like someone used to bowing under a low lintel.
new: Keep your hands in the torchlight, stranger. You stoop like someone used to low lintels.

speaker: Narrator
old: Stone dust coats the mason's knuckles, and his chisel taps a dry, steady warning against his leather apron.
new: Stone dust coats the mason's knuckles as his chisel taps a dry warning against his leather apron.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: I know that stoop. Every night since the frost set in, a crooked man stands at the foot of my bed and bends his neck the exact same way.
new: Every night since the frost, a crooked man at the foot of my bed bends his neck that exact way.

speaker: Player
old: I knelt in the ashes once, mason, before I knew what was waiting behind the branches. I am done kneeling.
new: I knelt in the ashes once, mason, before I knew what waited behind the branches. I am done kneeling.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: Are you now? That is easy to say in the square with lanterns burning, and harder when the thatch starts whispering at three in the morning.
new: Easy to say by lantern light. Harder when the thatch whispers at three in the morning.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: Damp gets in the knees, traveler, not the soul. You know the cadence of the old litany, do not lie to a man who cuts headstones.
new: Damp gets in the knees, not the soul. You know the old litany, do not lie to a headstone cutter.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: In the dream, the Crooked Man counts his servants on long, knotted fingers. Three names belong to the coven out in the timber, and their sign is carved under my eaves.
new: In the dream, the Crooked Man counts his servants. Three names belong to the timber coven, their sign carved under my eaves.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: Maybe a runaway hound is best for hunting the pack. Come talk to me by the yard when the square clears, and we will trade names.
new: A runaway hound is best for hunting the pack. Meet me by the yard when the square clears to trade names.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: Do not rub at your eyes like that, dear, you will only make the bruising darker. Printer's gall and graveyard tallow leave a very specific stain on the lids.
new: Do not rub your eyes, dear. Printer's gall and graveyard tallow leave a very specific stain.

speaker: Narrator
old: The bookseller smells of dry vellum, cloves, and mouse-chewed linen as she peers over her half-moon spectacles.
new: She peers over half-moon spectacles, smelling of dry vellum, cloves, and mouse-chewed linen.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: You have the sickness of the uncut folio. Someone has been reading chapters that were meant to stay sewn shut.
new: You have the uncut folio sickness. Someone has been reading chapters meant to stay sewn shut.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: Oh, delightful! Though the third edition corrects "parish" to "abbey" just before the censor's fire took the press.
new: Delightful! Though the third edition corrects "parish" to "abbey" just before the censor's fire took the press.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: Road dust washes off with cold water, my friend. A crooked footnote stays behind the brow-bone and ticks like a beetle in the wainscoting.
new: Road dust washes off. A crooked footnote stays behind the brow-bone, ticking like a beetle in the wall.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: My shelves here are mostly almanacs and harmless pastorals, for my health's sake. What you crave is split three ways: an island, a sunken library, and a dead bailiff's ledger.
new: I keep mostly almanacs and pastorals, for my health. What you crave is split between an island, a sunken library, and a dead bailiff's ledger.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: Come back when you have a quiet hour and a dry candle. It is a rare treat to meet another reader who knows books can bite.
new: Come back with a quiet hour and a dry candle. Few readers know books can bite.

speaker: weston_murdoch
old: Well now, bless the road and the mud upon it! Look at the weave of that cloak, neighbors, that is provincial wool if ever I saw a loom.
new: Bless the road! Look at that cloak, neighbors, provincial wool if ever I saw a loom.

speaker: Narrator
old: The preacher's voice rings out warm as spiced cider across the cold cobbles, his hands open and ungloved.
new: The preacher's voice rings warm as spiced cider across the cobbles, his hands ungloved.

speaker: weston_murdoch
old: You are no stranger to the crooked moon, friend, only new to our little hollow. Which province claimed your prayers before you walked into Wickermoor?
new: You know the crooked moon, friend, though you are new to Wickermoor. Which province claimed your prayers?

speaker: Player
old: "A sheaf for the rain, a stone for the gate, and a song for the bird that wakes too late." We sang it whenever the wagons came in whole.
new: "A sheaf for the rain, a stone for the gate, and a song for the bird that wakes too late." We sang it when wagons came in whole.

speaker: weston_murdoch
old: Ha! Hear that cadence! Three faiths braided into four bars of music, and not a sour note among them.
new: Ha! Three faiths braided into four bars of music, without a sour note.

speaker: weston_murdoch
old: That is the grand old way of the provinces. An oak bough over the barn, a sunflower on the table, and a songbird carved into the cradle.
new: The grand old provincial way. Oak bough over the barn, sunflower on the table, songbird on the cradle.

speaker: weston_murdoch
old: Ah, the road makes cynics of us all when the boots wear thin. Still, your tongue carries the rhythm of the old parish bells.
new: Thin boots make cynics of us all, yet your tongue keeps the rhythm of the old parish bells.

speaker: weston_murdoch
old: Our choir can always use a voice that knows Druskenvald is wider than one village square. Walk in grace, cousin, and my door is ever unlatched.
new: Our choir needs a voice that knows Druskenvald is wider than one square. Walk in grace, cousin, my door is unlatched.

speaker: Narrator
old: Iron keys clink against her belt, and the smell of cold tallow and scrubbed stone hangs round her like a cloak.
new: Iron keys clink at her belt, and she smells of cold tallow and scrubbed stone.

speaker: doris_squire
old: Three barred cells behind me, fines for brawling, banishment for grand theft. Spill blood in murder and the Mayor takes your head before the Oak of Many Faces.
new: Three cells behind me. Fines for brawling, banishment for grand theft, and for murder the Mayor takes your head before the Oak of Many Faces.

speaker: doris_squire
old: Good folk mostly, when they are not spooked by moor-fog or preaching at each other in the mud. Do your business before the late bells and stay on the lantern paths.
new: Good folk mostly, when not spooked by moor-fog or preaching in the mud. Finish your business before the late bells and stick to the lantern paths.

speaker: doris_squire
old: Every face in that bark was a name on the parish roll once. The roots drink deep after a sentence, and the moss stays red for a week.
new: Every face in that bark was on the parish roll once. After a sentence, the roots drink deep and the moss stays red for a week.

speaker: Narrator
old: Beneath a brass sunflower weight lies a scrap of foolscap written in neat verse about rain on quiet wheat.
new: Beneath a brass sunflower weight lies a scrap of neat verse about rain on quiet wheat.

speaker: doris_squire
old: Eyes on my face, traveler, not on my desk. A woman is allowed a bit of quiet ink between lockups.
new: Eyes on my face, traveler. A woman is allowed a bit of quiet ink between lockups.

speaker: doris_squire
old: The postmaster is the post. Without more than that, I do not touch her. Mind what you say of her.
new: The postmaster is the post. Bring more than that, and mind what you say of her.

speaker: Narrator
old: Tall stacks of calfskin folios lean like chimneys around a desk cluttered with crusted inkwells. A gaunt woman squints at you over wire-rimmed spectacles, a smudge of gall ink across her chin.
new: Calfskin folios lean like chimneys around a cluttered desk. A gaunt woman with gall ink on her chin squints over wire-rimmed spectacles.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: If you are looking for almanacs, third shelf on the left, mind the loose floorboard. And please do not slam the door, Sheridan has just got the kettle to boil.
new: Almanacs are third shelf on the left, mind the loose board. And do not slam the door, Sheridan just boiled the kettle.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: I deal in vellum, iron-gall ink, and verified histories, see Grimshaw's Third Compendium, page forty-two. I refuse to part with a single volume until I have read it cover to cover myself.
new: I sell vellum, iron-gall ink, and verified histories, see Grimshaw's Third Compendium, page forty-two. I read every volume before I part with it.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: My late sister left me three children to raise in this damp hollow. In truth, Margery and Algernon do most of the minding when I lose track of the clocktower bells.
new: My late sister left me three children to raise. Margery and Algernon do most of the minding when I miss the clocktower bells.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: Wipe your hands on your coat first, if you please. The parchment is dry, and the ink is freshly mixed.
new: Wipe your hands first, please. The parchment is dry and the ink freshly mixed.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: The parish records before the seventy-third year have had their bindings cut with a pruning knife. Someone in Wickermoor is very keen that we forget who planted that oak in the Round.
new: Someone took a pruning knife to the parish records before the seventy-third year, keen that we forget who planted the oak in the Round.

speaker: Narrator
old: The letters on her desk do not merely sit on the page: they squirm toward her ink-stained fingertips like iron filings to a lodestone, leaving faint frost on the blotter.
new: The letters on her desk squirm toward her ink-stained fingertips like iron to a lodestone, leaving frost on the blotter.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: Close the cover, quickly. Some chapters in Druskenvald read you back once you've given them your candlelight, and they never let you sleep.
new: Close it, quickly. Some chapters in Druskenvald read you back by candlelight and never let you sleep.

speaker: Narrator
old: She snaps a heavy ledger shut over her notes, sending up a small puff of paper dust and dried lavender.
new: She snaps a ledger shut over her notes, raising a puff of dust and dried lavender.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: Private correspondence and tallies, nothing for the public shelf. My eyes are simply tired from the small print.
new: Private correspondence and tallies. My eyes are simply tired from the small print.

speaker: Narrator
old: Damp heather clings to the hem of an old wool coat. Above the stump, a sleek black crow watches you with one bright, yellow eye.
new: Damp heather clings to an old wool coat. Above the stump, a black crow watches you with one yellow eye.

speaker: brother_elias
old: Keep your tracts and your tithes in your pockets, travelers. I hold fast to the sacred doctrine of Absolutely Nothing, and I pray to it twice before breakfast.
new: Keep your tracts and tithes. I hold to the sacred doctrine of Absolutely Nothing, and pray to it twice before breakfast.

speaker: brother_elias
old: A leaky pine lean-to is temple enough for a mind swept clean of superstition. Though if the butcher's wife leaves salted pork by my stone, I am no fanatic to let it spoil.
new: A leaky pine lean-to suffices for a mind clean of superstition. Though if the butcher's wife leaves salted pork by my stone, I will not let it spoil.

speaker: brother_elias
old: Hold your tongue, you feathered deacon! He claims I bowed my head when the thunder cracked last night, when I was merely looking for my spectacles.
new: Hush, you feathered deacon! He claims I bowed at the thunder last night, when I was just looking for my spectacles.

speaker: brother_elias
old: Worst are the fools carving antlers on hares in the dark, as if a rabbit did not have trouble enough getting down its hole.
new: Worst are the fools carving antlers on hares in the dark, as if rabbits had not trouble enough getting down their holes.

speaker: Narrator
old: The Trading Post smells of tallow and damp wool, with a polished brass scale gleaming on the counter.
new: The Trading Post smells of tallow and damp wool, a brass scale gleaming on the counter.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: A merchant lives by honest measure, friends, yet Eleanor Heyling sells fine rag paper across the Round for less than the mill charges. Glance at her ledger for me, and learn how she keeps her purse full.
new: Eleanor Heyling sells fine rag paper across the Round for less than the mill charges. Glance at her ledger and see how she keeps her purse full.

speaker: Narrator
old: Dry parchment and walnut gall scent the narrow shelves, and an open account book rests beside Eleanor's elbow.
new: Dry parchment and walnut gall scent the shelves, an open account book beside Eleanor's elbow.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: If Baltus sent you to whine about vellum, tell him to scrape the lead out from under his brass scale first. Have you come to read, or just to hover?
new: If Baltus sent you to whine about vellum, tell him to scrape the lead from under his brass scale first. Come to read, or just to hover?

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: Every pound of lampblack ink from his counter weighs fourteen ounces by any honest iron. I price my sheets so the schoolhouse does not have to beg him for scraps.
new: A pound of his lampblack ink weighs fourteen ounces by honest iron. I price my sheets so the schoolhouse needn't beg him for scraps.

speaker: Narrator
old: {name} traces the neat red ink along the margin: the loss on every quire is covered by a quiet newcomer fund signed by Finneas Trout.
new: {name} traces the red margin ink: a newcomer fund signed by Finneas Trout covers the loss on every quire.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
old: This book is not for sale, stranger. If you want sums, bother Tamsin Ledger up at the Mayor's House.
new: This book is not for sale. If you want sums, bother Tamsin Ledger at the Mayor's House.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
old: Two merchants accusing each other of arithmetic is the dullest sin in Wickermoor. For ten gold to cover my candles, I will audit both books before the sixth bell.
new: Two merchants arguing arithmetic is Wickermoor's dullest sin. For ten gold in candles, I will audit both books before the sixth bell.

speaker: Narrator
old: By next candle-mark, Tamsin lays a single sheet of foolscap on the desk, smelling faintly of cold tea.
new: By next candle-mark, Tamsin lays down a single sheet of foolscap, smelling of cold tea.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
old: Baltus thumbs his brass pan by two drams, and Eleanor covers her cheap paper with a schoolhouse grant from Finneas Trout. Both books balance, if you squint.
new: Baltus thumbs his brass pan by two drams; Eleanor covers her cheap paper with a schoolhouse grant from Finneas Trout. Both books balance, if you squint.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: You have the look of folks who have seen the bottom of the inkwell. Come, how do we settle our dear neighbour?
new: You look like folks who have seen the bottom of the inkwell. How do we settle our dear neighbour?

speaker: baltus_tolliver
old: A schoolhouse grant from poor Finneas? Wait until the Round hears the newcomers need charity just to write a letter.
new: A schoolhouse grant from Finneas? Wait till the Round hears the newcomers need charity just to write a letter.

speaker: holly_aster
old: Dust your boots and listen close, newcomers. Tomorrow is the Founders' feast, and Siv Harga thinks her greasy sausage rolls belong at the high table instead of my spiced harvest loaf.
new: Listen close, newcomers. Tomorrow is the Founders' feast, and Siv Harga thinks her greasy sausage rolls belong at the high table over my spiced harvest loaf.

speaker: holly_aster
old: Carry this warm loaf to Mayor Somerton and speak well of my crust. And sneak a bite of Siv's pastry first, then tell me true if her suet beats my cinnamon.
new: Take this warm loaf to Mayor Somerton and praise my crust. Sneak a bite of Siv's pastry first, and tell me if her suet beats my cinnamon.

speaker: siv_harga
old: Holly Aster sent you sniffing round my chopping block, did she? That woman bakes dry sawdust and calls it sacred custom.
new: Holly Aster sent you sniffing round my block? That woman bakes dry sawdust and calls it sacred custom.

speaker: siv_harga
old: Try one of my pork rolls before you judge, fresh from the tin. Better yet, carry a tray up to Mayor Somerton and tell him real meat beats sweet dough.
new: Try a pork roll first, fresh from the tin. Better yet, take a tray to Mayor Somerton and tell him real meat beats sweet dough.

speaker: Narrator
old: The pastry flakes at the first bite, rich with sage, black pepper, and clean pork fat. You have to admit it is remarkably good.
new: The pastry flakes at first bite, rich with sage, black pepper, and clean pork fat. It is remarkably good.

speaker: Narrator
old: The mayor samples a crumb of spiced crust and a corner of warm pastry, wiping his chin with a linen napkin.
new: The mayor samples the spiced crust and warm pastry, wiping his chin with a linen napkin.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Oh, dear me, both are splendid, yet tradition demands a single crown dish. Which baker claims your vote?
new: Both are splendid, yet tradition demands a single crown dish. Which baker claims your vote?

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: By the Oak, what wisdom! Savory meat in the left hand, sweet bread in the right! We shall raise a toast to harmony!
new: By the Oak, what wisdom! Savory meat in the left hand, sweet bread in the right! A toast to harmony!

speaker: Narrator
old: While the mayor turns to fetch his goblet, {name} tips a heavy cellar of coarse salt straight into Siv's gravy seam. Siv will never know whose hand ruined the batch.
new: While the mayor fetches his goblet, {name} tips coarse salt straight into Siv's gravy seam. She will never know who ruined the batch.

speaker: Narrator
old: Lanterns swing above the long trestle tables as Ambrose Quill rises, clearing his throat with terrifying authority.
new: Lanterns swing above the trestle tables as Ambrose Quill rises and clears his throat.

speaker: ambrose_quill
old: O blessed feast of Wickermoor, where crumbs fall down to sweep the floor more! May bad meat never make us sicker, nor empty tankards drain the quicker!
new: O blessed feast of Wickermoor, where crumbs fall down to sweep the floor! May bad meat never make us sicker, nor empty tankards drain the quicker!

speaker: finneas_trout
old: Welcome to the schoolhouse. I am Finneas Trout, and I am trying to teach these children history without giving them nightmares, which is rather difficult in Wickermoor.
new: Welcome to the schoolhouse. I am Finneas Trout. Teaching these children history without giving them nightmares is rather difficult in Wickermoor.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: Could you help me gather five small lessons about the Founder? Things they can hold: Pip Oakum's button, a fact from Old Rusty, a bell-rope thread, and a church chalk mark.
new: Help me gather five small lessons on the Founder: Pip Oakum's button, a fact from Old Rusty, a bell-rope thread, and a church chalk mark.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: As for the fifth lesson, come back to me once you have the first four. I will explain it then.
new: Come back once you have those four, and I will explain the fifth.

speaker: pip_oakum
old: You want a Founder's button for Mr. Trout? That is brass from an old coat, mister, and brass costs a true story from before you came here.
new: A Founder's button for Mr. Trout? That is old coat brass, mister, and it costs a true story from before you came here.

speaker: pip_oakum
old: You muddled the middle bit, and your voice went all squeaky at the end. Take the button anyway, before Mr. Trout frets himself grey.
new: You muddled the middle and went squeaky at the end. Take the button anyway, before Mr. Trout frets himself grey.

speaker: old_rusty
old: A lesson for the little ones, is it? Tell them the Founder was mortal terrified of Tuesdays, bolted his shutters tight, and nobody living recalls why.
new: A lesson for the little ones? The Founder was mortal terrified of Tuesdays and bolted his shutters tight, though nobody living recalls why.

speaker: Narrator
old: Above the dusty stones, the clocktower bell-rope hangs frayed and heavy with old tallow. Solomon Roderick stands nearby, wiping stone dust from his knuckles.
new: The clocktower bell-rope hangs frayed and heavy with tallow. Solomon Roderick stands nearby, wiping stone dust from his knuckles.

speaker: solomon_roderick
old: Just a single hemp strand for the schoolhouse? Help yourself, friend, the bell will toll the hours all the same without it.
new: One hemp strand for the schoolhouse? Help yourself, friend. The bell will toll the hours all the same.

speaker: Narrator
old: Your boot slips on the slick timber, leaving you with a scraped knee and empty hands. Solomon will gladly hand over a thread if you only ask.
new: Your boot slips on slick timber, leaving you with a scraped knee and empty hands. Just ask Solomon for a thread.

speaker: Narrator
old: Low on the church stones, half washed away by the moorland damp, someone has sketched a white chalk hare with branching antlers.
new: Low on the damp church stones, someone has sketched a white chalk hare with branching antlers.

speaker: Narrator
old: You trace the strange horned creature onto a scrap of slate, catching the gritty dust of the old lime on your fingertips.
new: You trace the horned creature onto a slate scrap, catching gritty lime dust on your fingertips.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: You brought all four, and the children are already passing the button around. Now for the fifth thing, the only one that truly matters to me.
new: You brought all four. Now for the fifth thing, the only one that truly matters.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: Please, stand before the class and tell them the Oak of Many Faces is only an ordinary tree. They are too young for what this village worships.
new: Tell the class the Oak of Many Faces is just an ordinary tree. They are too young for what this village worships.

speaker: Narrator
old: The schoolroom falls dead quiet, save for the ticking slate pencil in the back row. Then a small girl asks why the bark is still thirsty.
new: The schoolroom falls quiet save for a ticking slate pencil. Then a small girl asks why the bark is still thirsty.

speaker: Narrator
old: Finneas opens his mouth, looks toward the window where the crooked branches lean, and says nothing at all. The children understand the silence better than words.
new: Finneas looks toward the crooked branches outside and says nothing. The children understand the silence better than words.

speaker: Narrator
old: Ink, damp paper, and tallow smoke cling to the young man's cuffs as he adjusts his spectacles. He peers at you with the bright, restless posture of a city lecturer.
new: Ink, damp paper, and tallow smoke cling to the young man's cuffs. He adjusts his spectacles, bright and restless as a city lecturer.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: Good evening! Strangers from beyond the mist, unless I miss my guess, and wide awake besides. I am Finneas Trout of Baskerton, presently instructing this village in basic reason.
new: Good evening! Wide-awake strangers from beyond the mist, I gather. I am Finneas Trout of Baskerton, teaching this village basic reason.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: I lodge at the inn and spend my hours persuading children that thunder is weather, not an angry spirit. Mayor Somerton means well, though his fondness for old customs tries my patience.
new: I lodge at the inn and teach children that thunder is weather, not an angry spirit. Mayor Somerton means well, though his love of old customs tries my patience.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: I have been charting a malady called the Grey, where folk lose colour and heart until they fade into stupor. Superstition blames curses, yet every affliction has a mechanism.
new: I am charting the Grey, a malady where folk lose colour and heart until they fade into stupor. Superstition blames curses, yet every affliction has a mechanism.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: Odd that you are here, because I could swear I saw the spitting image of one of your party walk past the inn before the recent murders began. The likeness was uncanny.
new: I could swear I saw the spitting image of one of your party pass the inn before the recent murders began.

speaker: Narrator
old: Half a dozen beeswax tapers sit wrapped in neat twine beside his inkwell, far more than one small room requires.
new: Half a dozen beeswax tapers sit wrapped in twine beside his inkwell, far more than one small room needs.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: Oh, those are from Oswick Frey's chandlery, as I happen to read late and require reliable light. Mr. Frey is a remarkably thoughtful conversationalist for such a rustic parish.
new: Those are from Oswick Frey's chandlery, as I read late. Mr. Frey is a remarkably thoughtful conversationalist for such a rustic parish.

speaker: finneas_trout
old: A scholar goes through a dreadful number of candles in a realm without a sunrise, I assure you.
new: A scholar goes through a dreadful number of candles in a realm without a sunrise.

speaker: Narrator
old: A young woman in ink-stained cuffs taps a brass nib against a tall ledger, her brow furrowed at the wainscoted ceiling.
new: A young woman in ink-stained cuffs taps a brass nib against a tall ledger, frowning at the wainscoted ceiling.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
old: State your names and dates of decease if you are on the parish rolls. I am auditing Wickermoor's municipal assets, and the bookkeeping here is frankly irregular.
new: State your names and dates of decease for the parish rolls. I am auditing Wickermoor's municipal assets, and the bookkeeping is frankly irregular.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
old: Everything from turnip tithes to that screaming timber out on the Round, all in triplicate. They listed six public beheadings under seasonal pruning, which is a clear misallocation of county funds.
new: From turnip tithes to that screaming timber on the Round, all in triplicate. Listing six public beheadings under seasonal pruning is a clear misallocation of county funds.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
old: The Oak of Many Faces lacks a valid arboricultural permit and refuses to sign a declaration of sap. I have served a polite notice of eviction to its lower branches and asked it to vacate by the third bell.
new: The Oak of Many Faces lacks an arboricultural permit and refuses to sign a declaration of sap. I served its lower branches notice to vacate by the third bell.

speaker: Narrator
old: By the water trough, a whiskered veteran in a faded tunic polishes a dented breastplate with a clump of dry hay.
new: By the water trough, a whiskered veteran polishes a dented breastplate with a clump of dry hay.

speaker: sgt_gaunt
old: Stand at ease, travellers, you are looking at the hero of the Bramble Ford skirmish. When the bog-hounds breached the dyke, I executed a brisk tactical retreat of four miles to preserve my strategic judgement.
new: Stand at ease, travellers, before the hero of Bramble Ford. When bog-hounds breached the dyke, I executed a brisk four-mile tactical retreat to preserve my strategic judgement.

speaker: sgt_gaunt
old: At Hollow Pike I outran three phantom riders to warn the rear guard, and at Crooked Fen I held a turnip cellar from the inside for forty hours. I was always three steps from making a glorious stand, had the ground not been so damp.
new: At Hollow Pike I outran three phantom riders, and at Crooked Fen I held a turnip cellar from inside for forty hours. Only damp ground kept me from a glorious stand.

speaker: sgt_gaunt
old: Say the word and old Gaunt will march at the very front of the rear column. Wait, did that hay-wain just creak, step ahead of me and draw your steel while I guard your backs from behind the trough.
new: Say the word and old Gaunt marches at the very front of the rear column. Wait, did that hay-wain creak? Draw your steel while I guard your backs from behind the trough.

speaker: Narrator
old: A knee-high boy sits on the cold well-curb, rattling a tin cup full of horn, bone, and brass buttons like a miser's purse.
new: A knee-high boy sits on the cold well-curb, rattling a tin cup of horn, bone, and brass buttons.

speaker: pip_oakum
