old: Mind the puddle, strangers, you will splash the stock. You can keep your soft silver, because nothing holds a coat or a bargain together like a proper four-hole bone button.
new: Mind the puddle, strangers, you will splash the stock. Keep your soft silver; nothing holds a coat or a bargain together like a four-hole bone button.

speaker: pip_oakum
old: This pearl one fell off Postmaster Mayville's cuff, and the pewter hare is from Mayor Somerton's Sunday waistcoat. Constable Squire still owes me two brass anchors from her greatcoat, and I aim to collect.
new: This pearl one fell off Postmaster Mayville's cuff, and the pewter hare is from Mayor Somerton's Sunday waistcoat. Constable Squire still owes me two brass anchors from her greatcoat.

speaker: pip_oakum
old: That is genuine ash-wood off Undertaker Shade's third-best gaiters, slightly chewed by a stoat. Spend it wisely, friend, you are holding prime Wickermoor currency now.
new: That is genuine ash-wood off Undertaker Shade's third-best gaiters, slightly stoat-chewed. Spend it wisely; you hold prime Wickermoor currency.

speaker: granny_orla_pike
old: Keep your boots still if you mean to hover by my blankets. The fevered ones need a straight tune to sleep by, and this room is already full of folks who breathe off-key.
new: Keep your boots still by my blankets. The fevered ones need a straight tune to sleep, and this room is full of folks breathing off-key.

speaker: granny_orla_pike
old: Am I a clockwork lark to pipe up whenever a stranger rattles the latch? Give me a verse of your own first, and let me hear whether you have a throat or a rusted hinge.
new: Am I a clockwork lark to pipe up whenever a stranger rattles the latch? Give me a verse first, so I hear whether you have a throat or a rusted hinge.

speaker: granny_orla_pike
old: Flat on the turn, rushed at the cadence, and you swallowed the third word whole. Listen here, you hopeless magpie, it goes like this.
new: Flat on the turn, rushed at the cadence, and you swallowed the third word. Listen here, you hopeless magpie, it goes like this.

speaker: Narrator
old: Almost against her will, she hums the same verse back through toothless gums, turning it rich and steady as hearth smoke.
new: She hums the same verse back through toothless gums, rich and steady as hearth smoke.

speaker: Narrator
old: Turpentine and wet linen hang sharp in the air around a young man whose sparse beard is flecked with dry ochre.
new: Turpentine and wet linen hang sharp around a young man with dry ochre flecking his sparse beard.

speaker: gaston_doray
old: Hold still, your faces still have the grey rind of the river on them. Tell me, what is the colour of a sound when a bell drowns in fog?
new: Hold still, your faces still wear the grey rind of the river. Tell me, what colour is the sound of a bell drowning in fog?

speaker: gaston_doray
old: I walked out of the mist three years back with an empty head and a full brush. Look too long at a face and it lies, so I paint what sleeps behind the ribs.
new: I walked out of the mist three years back with an empty head and a full brush. Faces lie, so I paint what sleeps behind the ribs.

speaker: gaston_doray
old: Provincial theater, all of it. They carve wooden mouths into an old oak and call it holiness, though the red mud beneath its roots has a lovely, greedy sheen.
new: Provincial theater. They carve wooden mouths into an old oak and call it holiness, though the red mud beneath its roots has a lovely, greedy sheen.

speaker: gaston_doray
old: Something scratches inside the woods past the lantern-line, older than the Mayor's Green Queen. When the wind drops, you can hear branches growing in the dark like antlers.
new: Something older than the Mayor's Green Queen scratches in the woods past the lantern-line. When the wind drops, you hear branches growing in the dark like antlers.

speaker: Narrator
old: Deep in the indigo brushwork of every single canvas, a long-eared hare stares back from the thicket, crowned with bone-white prongs.
new: Deep in the indigo brushwork of every canvas, a hare crowned with bone-white prongs stares from the thicket.

speaker: gaston_doray
old: Strange, is it not? My wrist puts that little beast in the brambles before I even wake, and I dare not scrape it out.
new: Strange, is it not? My wrist paints that little beast in the brambles before I wake, and I dare not scrape it out.

speaker: Narrator
old: A breathless young woman sorts stacks of tied letters with ink-stained fingers, her leather satchel still damp from the moorland mist.
new: A breathless young woman sorts tied letters with ink-stained fingers, her leather satchel still damp from the mist.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: Oh, good evening! You caught me right between runs. Miss Theodora lets me mind the counter whenever I'm not out walking the valley roads.
new: Good evening! You caught me between runs. Miss Theodora lets me mind the counter when I'm not walking the valley roads.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: Look at my eyes, lilac as spring heather. The village grandmothers used to cross their fingers at me and mutter about bad luck.
new: Look at my eyes, lilac as spring heather. The village grandmothers used to cross their fingers and mutter about bad luck.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: Miss Theodora took me in and told me a rare colour is a gift, not a curse. I owe her my whole living.
new: Miss Theodora took me in and called a rare colour a gift, not a curse. I owe her my living.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: Wickermoor is safe enough inside the lanterns, though Mayor Somerton's folk can be stern about the old customs. Once you pass the Founder's Round, though, the mist plays tricks on the footpaths.
new: Wickermoor is safe inside the lanterns, though Mayor Somerton's folk are stern about the old customs. Past the Founder's Round, the mist plays tricks on the footpaths.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: Whatever you do, don't whistle after the clocktower strikes the third hour. The birds in the rafters get terribly restless when folks whistle out of tune.
new: Don't whistle after the clocktower strikes the third hour. The birds in the rafters get terribly restless when folks whistle out of tune.

speaker: Narrator
old: Her thumb worries the corner of an opened envelope addressed in her own neat hand, though the ink inside has been scraped and rewritten.
new: Her thumb worries an opened envelope addressed in her own neat hand, its ink scraped and rewritten.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: It's nothing, truly, only I wrote to my cousin in the low valley last month, and the reply speaks of a quarrel we never had. Even the seal feels cold, like tallow.
new: I wrote to my cousin in the low valley last month, and the reply speaks of a quarrel we never had. Even the seal feels cold, like tallow.

speaker: Narrator
old: Ned Cooper the woodcutter lies among the roots of the Oak of Many Faces, his head set neatly beside his boots. The carved faces in the bark glisten dark and wet where the soil has drunk its fill.
new: Ned Cooper the woodcutter lies among the roots of the Oak of Many Faces, his head set neatly by his boots. Above the sated soil, the bark's carved faces glisten dark and wet.

speaker: mori_shade
old: The dead speak only once, travelers. I have shown you all poor Ned brought to my table.
new: The dead speak only once, travelers. Here is all poor Ned brought to my table.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Poor Ned held tight to the end. When I pried his cold fingers open, I found this coarse grey hair, long as a widow's shawl.
new: When I pried poor Ned's cold fingers open, I found this coarse grey hair, long as a widow's shawl.

speaker: mori_shade
old: And look here upon his palm. Two tiny crossed axes, seared into the flesh with hot iron. The old mark of Gus Strong's apprentice.
new: Look upon his palm: two tiny crossed axes seared into the flesh. The mark of Gus Strong's apprentice.

speaker: beatrice_wells
old: Sold one two nights past to Marta Dunn, a quiet widow in black. Said her hearthwood was terribly knotted, poor dear.
new: Sold one two nights past to Marta Dunn, a quiet widow in black. Said her hearthwood was terribly knotted.

speaker: Narrator
old: The damp air of the churchyard smells of turned earth and cold iron. Marta Dunn rests her hands upon the haft of a broad, gleaming felling axe.
new: The damp churchyard smells of turned earth and cold iron. Marta Dunn rests her hands on a broad, gleaming felling axe.

speaker: marta_dunn
old: Do not fret for Ned, my dears. Gus taught me how to make the stroke swift and kind, so the old oak never has to thirst.
new: Do not fret for Ned, my dears. Gus taught me a swift, kind stroke, so the old oak never thirsts.

speaker: marta_dunn
old: You have sharp eyes, youngsters. Yes, I kept Gus's brand, and I keep his duty. Wickermoor has forgotten its debts to the roots, so someone must pay the tally.
new: Sharp eyes, youngsters. I kept Gus's brand and his duty. Wickermoor forgot its debts to the roots, so someone must pay the tally.

speaker: marta_dunn
old: An old woman has many chores in a cold season, my dears. Pay no mind to an old widow's hands.
new: An old widow has many chores in a cold season, my dears. Pay no mind to my hands.

speaker: marta_dunn
old: Bless you for asking kindly, truly. Give yourself to Doris's rope when the roots are still dry? No, my dears, the work is not half done.
new: Bless you for asking kindly. Give myself to Doris's rope while the roots are still dry? No, my dears, the work is not half done.

speaker: randall_graham
old: Trim or a bloodletting, friends? Only, I am in a strange pinch. Swept-up locks from my floor keep turning up in the undertaker's cellar, and I cannot fathom how.
new: Trim or a bloodletting, friends? Swept-up locks from my floor keep turning up in the undertaker's cellar, and I cannot fathom how.

speaker: randall_graham
old: Every lock down there belongs to a fellow who took a sudden, rattling chill the week after his trim. Folk are starting to eye my scissors crooked.
new: Every lock down there belongs to a fellow who took a rattling chill the week after his trim. Folk are eyeing my scissors crooked.

speaker: Narrator
old: Behind a crate of tonic bottles sits a tall glass jar, stuffed with ribboned locks of hair and paper slips.
new: Behind a crate of tonic bottles sits a glass jar stuffed with ribboned hair and paper slips.

speaker: Narrator
old: Each slip bears a customer's name and a date falling on the dark of the moon, matching the Order's monthly tithe to the letter.
new: Each slip bears a customer's name and a dark-moon date, matching the Order's monthly tithe.

speaker: Narrator
old: Damp cellar rot and a broad thumbprint of tallow ink have blurred the dates beyond reading. Whatever the pattern is, it may show clearer at the funeral home.
new: Cellar rot and tallow ink have blurred the dates. The pattern may show clearer at the funeral home.

speaker: Narrator
old: On a cold stone shelf beside an unchiseled coffin plate rests a stoppered jar of hair, tied with the very same barber's twine.
new: Beside an unchiseled coffin plate rests a jar of hair, tied with the same barber's twine.

speaker: randall_graham
old: Do not say it aloud! I owed the Order a steep sum from a bad winter, and they took payment in clippings. I never knew why they wanted them, I swear it.
new: Do not say it aloud! I owed the Order a steep sum from a bad winter, and they took payment in clippings. I swear I never knew why.

speaker: randall_graham
old: Fifty coin, just like that? You have lifted a millstone off my windpipe, friends. I will sweep my floor straight into the stove from this hour on.
new: Fifty coin, just like that? You have lifted a millstone off my windpipe. I will sweep my floor straight into the stove from now on.

speaker: Narrator
old: When he tells her at the barracks door, Doris only sighs through her nose and sets the kettle on, gentle as forged steel can be.
new: At the barracks door, Doris only sighs and sets the kettle on, gentle as forged steel.

speaker: randall_graham
old: Mum's the word, then. Take these few coins, and here, a curl from my own crown, so we are bound fair and square.
new: Mum's the word, then. Take these coins and a curl from my own crown, so we are bound fair and square.

speaker: Narrator
old: Woodsmoke and dried blood drift from the heavy pelts across her shoulders as she tests a broadhead arrow against her thumb.
new: Woodsmoke and dried blood drift from her pelts as she tests a broadhead arrow against her thumb.

speaker: hilda_brom
old: You walk loud enough to wake every crow between here and the bog. State your business quick, or step out of my light.
new: You walk loud enough to wake every crow to the bog. State your business quick, or step out of my light.

speaker: hilda_brom
old: Ha, got coin after all? Take your pick of smoked haunch and winter fur, or hire my boots if you fear the mire.
new: Ha, got coin after all? Pick from smoked haunch and winter fur, or hire my boots if you fear the mire.

speaker: hilda_brom
old: Somerton pays me to drag runaways back to the Oak of Many Faces. Once a trail is warm, nothing on two legs or four shakes me off.
new: Somerton pays me to drag runaways back to the Oak of Many Faces. Once a trail is warm, nothing shakes me off.

speaker: hilda_brom
old: Town folk huddle by their bonfires, praying the dark stays out. Me, I keep the Green Queen's custom: take only what bleeds, and leave the heart for the roots.
new: Town folk huddle by bonfires, praying the dark stays out. I keep the Green Queen's custom: take only what bleeds, and leave the heart for the roots.

speaker: hilda_brom
old: There is a great spirit bear walking the deep ridge, calling me to shed my skin and run on four paws forever. Some nights I want to answer, and that freezes my marrow.
new: A great spirit bear walks the deep ridge, calling me to shed my skin and run on four paws. Some nights I want to answer, and that freezes my marrow.

speaker: Narrator
old: Warm cinnamon and browned butter pour from the bakehouse door. Holly wipes flour from her apron with quick, restless fingers, her cheeks flushed red from the brick ovens.
new: Warm cinnamon and browned butter pour from the bakehouse. Flushed from the brick ovens, Holly wipes flour from her apron with restless fingers.

speaker: holly_aster
old: Violet braids the dough-rings now, and little Lavender puts the cloves in the tarts. Siv keeps the hearth stacked and the house steady when my head gets spinning.
new: Violet braids the dough-rings, and little Lavender cloves the tarts. Siv keeps the hearth stacked and the house steady when my head spins.

speaker: holly_aster
old: I leave the first loaf of every batch at the roots of the Oak for the Green Queen. The Old Ways kept this village fed long before we got here, and I won't have my girls forgetting their manners.
new: I leave every first loaf at the Oak's roots for the Green Queen. The Old Ways kept this village fed, and my girls won't forget their manners.

speaker: holly_aster
old: The two grand folk from the estate rode past at early Twilight in their fine coat-cloth. When lords come down to the moor, it's always the village that pays the reckoning.
new: The two grand folk from the estate rode past at early Twilight. When lords come to the moor, it's always the village that pays the reckoning.

speaker: Narrator
old: Flour sifts from her shaking knuckles as she taps the kneading board in sets of seven, her lips moving without sound whenever the clocktower creaks.
new: Flour sifts from her shaking knuckles as she taps the board in sets of seven, lips moving soundlessly whenever the clocktower creaks.

speaker: holly_aster
old: Thirty-four loaves on the rack, and never room for one more. If a woman owes a debt she didn't sign for, all the prayers to the Oak won't stop the house from calling her number.
new: Thirty-four loaves on the rack, and never room for more. When a woman owes a debt she didn't sign for, prayers to the Oak won't stop the house calling her number.

speaker: howie_butterman
old: Evening to you, friends, and welcome to the Founder's Round. Deputy Howie Butterman at your service, here to keep the peace and point newcomers the right way.
new: Welcome to the Founder's Round, friends. Deputy Howie Butterman, here to keep the peace and point newcomers the right way.

speaker: howie_butterman
old: Constable Squire handles the heavy scowling and the cell keys, and I handle the friendly word on the cobbles. Folk tell old Howie things they would never say across a desk.
new: Constable Squire handles the scowling and cell keys; I handle the friendly word on the cobbles. Folk tell old Howie what they would never say across a desk.

speaker: howie_butterman
old: Most of us hold to the Old Ways and the oak in the square, though you will see sunflowers on a few lintels and songbird ribbons down the lane. It takes all sorts to fill a parish.
new: Most of us hold to the Old Ways and the square's oak, though you will see sunflowers on lintels and songbird ribbons down the lane.

speaker: howie_butterman
old: Now that you arrived with Lord Phillip and Lady Adela, things are bound to stir. If you fancy stretching your legs, the old barrow path past the heather has had strange lights all week.
new: Things will stir now you arrived with Lord Phillip and Lady Adela. The old barrow path past the heather has had strange lights all week.

speaker: Narrator
old: When he leans in, a dried hare's foot on a leather cord slips from under his collar, and his pulse jumps with bright, hungry excitement.
new: As he leans in, a dried hare's foot on a cord slips from his collar, his pulse jumping with hungry excitement.

speaker: howie_butterman
old: We have been waiting on proper travelers to walk in with the gentry. You mark my words, the woods are ready for a change of season.
new: We have been waiting on proper travelers to walk in with the gentry. Mark my words, the woods are ready for a change of season.

speaker: Narrator
old: Heat rolls from the hearth, smelling of quenched iron and coal smoke. The squat smith checks the edge of his neatly trimmed beard in a polished buckler.
new: Quenched iron and coal smoke roll from the hearth. The squat smith checks his trimmed beard in a polished buckler.

speaker: jean_myriel
old: Step in out of the damp, strangers. Whether you need a mule shod, a blade silvered, or a bit of gold twisted pretty, my anvil is hot.
new: Step out of the damp, strangers. Whether you need a mule shod, a blade silvered, or gold twisted pretty, my anvil is hot.

speaker: jean_myriel
old: Left my old mountain town by night because the elders called my scrollwork wicked. Here, so long as I mend their ploughshares, nobody asks why my candlesticks have thorns.
new: Left my mountain town by night because the elders called my scrollwork wicked. Here, so long as I mend ploughshares, nobody asks why my candlesticks have thorns.

speaker: jean_myriel
old: Half the town wants silver charms against the moor, and the other half wantspadlocks against their neighbours. Good business for a smith either way.
new: Half the town wants silver charms against the moor, and the other half wants padlocks against their neighbours. Good business either way.

speaker: jean_myriel
old: Sharp eyes. I learned my tempering among the Crimson Rose, where we quenched good steel in a drop of willing blood, though I stick to pig's blood here.
new: Sharp eyes. Among the Crimson Rose, we quenched good steel in willing blood, though I stick to pig's blood here.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
old: I speak for every spade and plough round this moor. Without our roots in the pot, Wickermoor starves, yet Somerton pays us in prayers to his oak.
new: I speak for every spade and plough on this moor. Without our roots in the pot, Wickermoor starves, yet Somerton pays us in prayers to his oak.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
old: The pumpkin-headed straw folk out Foxwillow way cannot pull a clean crop from the furrow. Something sours the soil, and the union will pay good silver to whoever sets it right.
new: The pumpkin-headed straw folk in Foxwillow cannot pull a clean crop. Something sours the soil, and the union will pay good silver to set it right.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
old: Fine timber and proud lanterns at the Founder's Round, paid for by folk with mud under their nails. Keep your eyes on your purse when the tithe-basket passes.
new: Fine timber and lanterns at the Founder's Round, paid for by folk with mud under their nails. Watch your purse when the tithe-basket passes.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
old: Well now, you have an honest grip to you. Tell the straw folk in Foxwillow that Jeremiah Stover sent you, and they will show you the blighted fields.
new: You have an honest grip. Tell the Foxwillow straw folk Jeremiah Stover sent you, and they will show you the blighted fields.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
old: Talk is cheap as chaff, friend. Put your boots in the mire out by Foxwillow first, then we can speak of fair wages.
new: Talk is cheap as chaff, friend. Put your boots in the Foxwillow mire first, then we can speak of fair wages.

speaker: Narrator
old: Loose paper sheets flutter in her hands, smelling of fresh printer's ink and lavender soap. Her beaming smile fixes on you before you can take a step back.
new: Loose sheets smelling of printer's ink and lavender soap flutter in her hands. Her beaming smile fixes on you before you can step back.

speaker: joan_murdoch
old: Oh, fresh faces in the square, praise the song! Take a hymn-sheet, take two, my husband Weston is just inside tuning up the rafters!
new: Fresh faces, praise the song! Take a hymn-sheet, my husband Weston is inside tuning up the rafters!

speaker: joan_murdoch
old: I copy every verse by candlelight while Peter and Charlotte practice their harmonies. If folk only hum the tune while churning butter, the light gets a foothold!
new: I copy verses by candlelight while Peter and Charlotte practice harmonies. If folk hum along while churning butter, the light gets a foothold!

speaker: joan_murdoch
old: People shut their shutters at first, bless them, they are shy as field mice. Give me another month of knocking and we will have every pew packed tight.
new: Folk shut their shutters at first, shy as mice. Give me a month of knocking and every pew will be packed.

speaker: joan_murdoch
old: Poor Mrs. Oakum from the butcher's shop bolted like a startled hare when I offered her a pamphlet at dusk. Half this town acts as though a kind word might bite.
new: Poor Mrs. Oakum at the butcher's bolted like a hare when I offered a pamphlet at dusk. Half this town acts like a kind word bites.

speaker: Narrator
old: For a breath her bright grin softens, and she smooths a crumpled corner of the songbook with ink-stained thumbs.
new: Her grin softens, and she smooths the songbook with ink-stained thumbs.

speaker: joan_murdoch
old: If we do not fill this town with music, the gloom will swallow my children whole. A mother will knock on every door in the realm before she lets the dark have her family.
new: Without music, the gloom will swallow my children whole. I will knock on every door in the realm before I let the dark have my family.

speaker: joan_murdoch
old: Why, because a good song is meant to be shared, dear heart! Keep that sheet dry in your pocket and sing it when the road gets long.
new: A good song is meant to be shared, dear heart! Keep that sheet dry and sing it when the road gets long.

speaker: Narrator
old: A cedar shelf holds a dead traveler's belongings: a brass button, dry boots, and a folded letter sealed with tallow.
new: A cedar shelf holds a dead traveler's brass button, dry boots, and a letter sealed with tallow.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Walder Pye came in on the rain cart and never rose again. That letter was dry inside his coat, waiting for someone with living feet.
new: Walder Pye came in on the rain cart and never rose. That letter stayed dry in his coat, waiting for living feet.

speaker: mori_shade
old: It is addressed to his kin past the border stones. Carry it past the gate yourself, if you please, for our post office cannot leave a dead man's final words untouched.
new: It goes to his kin past the border stones. Carry it past the gate yourself, or our post office will tamper with a dead man's final words.

speaker: theodora_mayville
old: Step up to the grate and declare your parcels. No written matter leaves Wickermoor during the quarantine without my stamp and inspection.
new: Step up and declare your parcels. No writing leaves Wickermoor during quarantine without my stamp and inspection.

speaker: theodora_mayville
old: How wise of you to trust the proper channels. Poor Walder's penmanship is dreadful, and his gloom would only upset his folk, so I shall improve it before the bag goes out.
new: Wise of you to use proper channels. Walder's penmanship is dreadful and his gloom would upset his folk, so I shall improve it first.

speaker: Narrator
old: `{name}` slides the tallow-sealed paper beneath a cuff just as the postmaster peers over her spectacles.
new: {name} slides the tallow-sealed paper beneath a cuff as the postmaster peers over her spectacles.

speaker: theodora_mayville
old: Empty hands and loitering boots. If you have no business with the post, clear the counter for those who can read a notice.
new: Empty hands and loitering boots. If you have no post business, clear the counter for those who can read.

speaker: theodora_mayville
old: Then do not breathe upon my brasswork. Stand aside and keep your hands where the parish can see them.
new: Then do not breathe on my brasswork. Stand aside and keep your hands where the parish can see them.

speaker: theodora_mayville
old: Unstamped correspondence concealed in a coat! Constable Squire, take these smugglers to the cells while I correct this wretched letter's tone.
new: Unstamped mail hid in a coat! Constable Squire, jail these smugglers while I correct this wretched letter's tone.

speaker: Narrator
old: Hilda tightens a leather girth strap by the moor road, her oilskin cloak smelling of wet heather and woodsmoke.
new: Hilda tightens a girth strap by the moor road, her oilskin cloak smelling of wet heather and smoke.

speaker: hilda_brom
old: Walder Pye's hand. He paid his tab and kept his dog quiet, so I will ride this out in my dry pack and drop it with the border carrier.
new: Walder Pye's hand. He paid his tab and kept his dog quiet, so I will ride this out in my dry pack to the border carrier.

speaker: lottery_stranger
old: Step right up, friends, and try your hand at the Founder's Round draw. Every folded slip in this hat holds a fair chance at a brighter season.
new: Step right up and try the Founder's Round draw. Every slip in this hat holds a fair chance at a brighter season.

speaker: Narrator
old: His grey coat is brushed clean of moorland dust, and the paper slips in his upturned hat rustle like dry leaves.
new: His grey coat is brushed clean, and the paper slips in his upturned hat rustle like dry leaves.

speaker: lottery_stranger
old: One hundred gold coins in a neat leather purse, paid on the spot. More than that, the winner enjoys a full year of effortless good fortune.
new: One hundred gold coins in a leather purse, paid on the spot, plus a full year of effortless good fortune.

speaker: lottery_stranger
old: A slip costs ten gold coins to draw from the hat. As for those who do not win, we simply cross their entry from the active roll and move along.
new: Ten gold coins a draw. If you do not win, we simply cross your name from the active roll.

speaker: lottery_stranger
old: Ah, an appreciation for tidy bookkeeping. I keep every participant's name in clean black ink so there is never a dispute.
new: Ah, a love for tidy bookkeeping. I record every name in clean black ink to prevent disputes.

speaker: Narrator
old: Dozens of local names are struck through with a ruler-straight line of wet black ink. When townsfolk pass by, their eyes slide right over those cottages as if no one ever lived there.
new: Dozens of local names are struck through in wet black ink. Passing townsfolk look right past those cottages as if no one ever lived there.

speaker: Narrator
old: The ledger bindings snap in your grip, scattering inked pages across the trodden mud of the square.
new: The ledger bindings snap in your grip, scattering inked pages across the mud.

speaker: lottery_stranger
old: Well now, that is one way to balance an account. Enjoy the rest of your evening in Wickermoor, travellers.
new: That is one way to balance an account. Enjoy your evening in Wickermoor, travellers.

speaker: Narrator
old: He steps back between two lantern-bearers, and by the time the smoke clears, his grey coat is nowhere to be seen.
new: He steps back between two lantern-bearers, and when the smoke clears, his grey coat is gone.

speaker: Narrator
old: The villagers around the square clap and cheer a bit too brightly, their smiles stretched tight in the lantern glow.
new: Villagers clap and cheer too brightly, smiles stretched tight in the lantern glow.

speaker: lottery_stranger
old: A blank slip, I am afraid, though I thank you for playing. Let me just tidy the register before you go.
new: A blank slip, I am afraid. Let me tidy the register before you go.

speaker: Narrator
old: His nib draws a single, cold black line through one of your names, and the air around your shoulders turns chill and thin.
new: His nib draws a cold black line through your name, and the air turns chill and thin.

speaker: lottery_stranger
old: Entirely your privilege, travellers. Should you find yourselves feeling luckier on another turn of the clock, you know where I stand.
new: Your privilege, travellers. Should you feel luckier on another turn of the clock, you know where I stand.

speaker: marianna_grey
old: The clocktower tolled and my grey mare Clover bolted straight up the northern moor road. Find her before the wolves do, and you will have my goodwill and three days free horse hire.
new: The clocktower tolled and my grey mare Clover bolted up the northern moor road. Find her before the wolves do for my goodwill and three days free horse hire.

speaker: marianna_grey
old: She is gentle as rain, just terribly skittish around flapping cloaks. Hold out a handful of dry oats and she will come right to your palm.
new: She is gentle, just skittish around flapping cloaks. Offer a handful of dry oats and she will come to your palm.

speaker: marianna_grey
old: Mind the ditches out there. The fog hides the ruts, and she has got only one good shoe on her forelegs.
new: Mind the ditches. Fog hides the ruts, and she has only one good front shoe.

speaker: marianna_grey
old: Empty halter in my hand and wind rising off the heather. Have you seen a hide or hair of her yet?
new: Empty halter in hand and wind rising. Seen hide or hair of her yet?

speaker: marianna_grey
old: Keep your cloaks tucked in and shake a pouch of oats if you get close. If the mud hides her prints, fetch Hilda Brom.
new: Tuck in your cloaks and shake a pouch of oats when close. If mud hides her prints, fetch Hilda Brom.

speaker: marianna_grey
old: I see. Best I latch the third stall shut then, and save the clean straw for the horses that are left.
new: I see. Best I latch the third stall shut and save the straw for the horses left.

speaker: Narrator
old: Deep, crescent hoofprints score the wet peat along the northern verge, filling slowly with black moor water.
new: Crescent hoofprints score the wet peat along the northern verge, filling with black moor water.

speaker: Narrator
old: Scuffed moss and snapped gorse stems mark a stumbling path toward a dark bramble thicket beside the north wall.
new: Scuffed moss and snapped gorse mark a stumbling path toward a bramble thicket by the north wall.

speaker: Narrator
old: The hoofprints vanish into a boggy churn of cart ruts and sheep droppings. Hilda Brom could read this mire better than you.
new: The hoofprints vanish into boggy cart ruts and sheep droppings. Hilda Brom could read this mire better.

speaker: hilda_brom
old: Thrown left shoe, panicked stride, dragging her halter rope through the gorse. Look in the thicket by the north wall.
new: Thrown left shoe, panicked stride, dragging her halter through the gorse. Check the thicket by the north wall.

speaker: Narrator
old: The dapple-grey mare stands tangled in wet briars by the stones, flanks heaving and ears pinned back at your shadow.
new: The dapple-grey mare stands tangled in wet briars by the stones, flanks heaving and ears pinned at your shadow.

speaker: Narrator
old: Her trembling eases at your touch, and she lowers her velvet nose enough for {name} to take the frayed halter rope.
new: Her trembling eases at your touch, and she lowers her nose for {name} to take the frayed rope.

speaker: Narrator
old: She snorts in terror, wrenching free of a briar to bolt a few yards down the wall. A handful of oats might steady her where quick hands failed.
new: She snorts in terror, wrenching free to bolt down the wall. A handful of oats might steady her where quick hands failed.

speaker: Narrator
old: The dry grain rustles in your palm, and the mare steps out of the thorns to lip the oats from {name}'s fingers.
new: Dry grain rustles in your palm, and the mare steps from the thorns to lip oats from {name}'s fingers.

speaker: Narrator
old: Clover presses her damp forehead against the stablemistress's shoulder, blowing a long, warm breath into her apron.
new: Clover presses her damp forehead to the stablemistress's shoulder, blowing a warm breath into her apron.

speaker: marianna_grey
old: Look at you, plastered in peat and burs, you foolish old girl. Take this coin for your trouble, friends, and any horse in my yard is yours free for three days.
new: Plastered in peat and burs, you foolish old girl. Take this coin, friends, and any horse in my yard is yours free for three days.

speaker: Narrator
old: Warm hay, liniment, and horse-sweat sweeten the dark of the stable, where a broad-shouldered woman braids a mule's mane with steady fingers.
new: Hay, liniment, and horse-sweat sweeten the dark stable, where a broad-shouldered woman braids a mule's mane.

speaker: marianna_grey
old: Two silver a night for stabling, brushed and fed right. I sleep up the ladder over the stalls, and a horse never lied to me yet.
new: Two silver a night for stabling, brushed and fed. I sleep over the stalls, and a horse never lied to me yet.

speaker: marianna_grey
old: Too much talk in the square about roots and blood for my liking. I keep a dried sunflower by the hayloft door and ask the Patient Lady for dry straw and quiet nights.
new: Too much talk in the square about roots and blood. I keep a dried sunflower by the hayloft and ask the Patient Lady for quiet nights.

speaker: marianna_grey
old: The mules come back from the north ditch lathered and shaking, with burrs twisted into knots no bramble ever made. Something out there runs on two legs and smells like winter.
new: The mules return from the north ditch lathered and shaking, burrs twisted in knots no bramble made. Something out there runs on two legs and smells like winter.

speaker: marianna_grey
old: Miss Alda acts sharp with her silver, sure, but she sends hot soup up my ladder when the frost bites and tells me to learn the inn's cellars. I do not know why she bothers with the likes of me.
new: Miss Alda acts sharp with her silver, but she sends up hot soup when frost bites and tells me to learn the inn's cellars. Don't know why she bothers with me.

speaker: Narrator
old: A big timber-framed house on the square opens its door, and a round man in a three-piece suit that strains at every button bustles out across the dirt, a cane in one hand and a bowler in the other.
new: A round man in a straining three-piece suit bustles out of a timber-framed house on the square, cane in one hand, bowler in the other.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Lord Phillip! Lady Adela! And what a way to be greeted. You have caught us in the middle of a very old custom, I'm afraid, and I do beg pardon for the commotion.
new: Lord Phillip! Lady Adela! Pardon the commotion. You've caught us in the middle of a very old custom, I'm afraid.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Quiet, my lord, quite, but for tonight. The oak drinks from the herds, once a year, so the hunting stays good and the barns stay full. A sacred tradition, nothing more.
new: Quiet, my lord, save for tonight. Once a year the oak drinks from the herds so the hunting stays good and the barns stay full. A sacred tradition, nothing more.

speaker: Narrator
old: He mops his bald head with a handkerchief and looks, for the first time, at the strangers who stood by and let the thing happen.
new: He mops his bald head and looks at the strangers who stood by and let it happen.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: And you, good travelers, were kind enough to let the rite alone. The Green Queen takes note of respect, and I shall see that the village does too.
new: And you, good travelers, kindly let the rite alone. The Green Queen notes respect, and I'll see the village does too.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Saved the little fellow, did you? Well, well. The oak will drink from the beasts of the field whatever you do, and a goat is a goat. We'll say no more of it.
new: Saved the little fellow, did you? Well, the oak will drink from the beasts whatever you do, and a goat is a goat. We'll say no more of it.

speaker: Narrator
old: His smile holds, but his handkerchief has gone to his forehead, and he does not stop mopping.
new: His smile holds, though he doesn't stop mopping his forehead.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Cut it loose, did you? The rite is the village's, you understand, and the Queen does not forgive a spoiled offering as easily as I do. I shall say a word to the neighbors.
new: Cut it loose, did you? The Queen does not forgive a spoiled offering as easily as I do. I shall say a word to the neighbors.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: A blood offering to the Green Queen, who keeps the Hollow's herds and hunts. Tradition, tradition. We've done it since before the clocktower, and the harvests have never once failed us.
new: A blood offering to the Green Queen, who keeps the Hollow's herds and hunts. We've done it since before the clocktower, and the harvests have never failed.

speaker: Narrator
old: His eyes slide to the east road and back, and a muscle jumps in his jaw. He is a man hiding something to please a lord.
new: His eyes slide toward the east road, a muscle jumping in his jaw. He's hiding something to please a lord.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Er. Some of our people have been, ah, taking sick lately. And a few have gone off without a word. Nothing to trouble his lordship with.
new: Er. Some folks have been taking sick lately, and a few have gone off without a word. Nothing to trouble his lordship with.

speaker: Narrator
old: He looks like exactly what he is, a mayor with a very good suit and a very full evening.
new: He looks like what he is: a mayor with a good suit and a full evening.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: The Druskenvald estate is quite ready for you, my lord. Pristine, staffed, a fine gift from the village. And for your friends, the Green Queen Inn, the one decent lodging in the Hollow. Alda Farnum keeps it.
new: The Druskenvald estate is ready, my lord. Pristine, staffed, a gift from the village. For your friends, Alda Farnum keeps the Green Queen Inn, the one decent lodging in the Hollow.

speaker: Narrator
old: The mayor's smile goes thin, and then goes altogether, and under it is a tired man in a tight suit.
new: The mayor's smile thins and vanishes, leaving a tired man in a tight suit.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: More disappearances, more fevers, more funerals than there ought to be. I'd rather not say more in front of the lord. Come to my office when it is open, and I will tell you what I know.
new: Too many disappearances, fevers, and funerals. Not in front of the lord, though. Come to my office when it's open.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Oh, I'm sure I don't know what you can mean. A village is a village, good people. It has its seasons.
new: I'm sure I don't know what you mean. A village has its seasons, good people.

speaker: phillip_druskenvald
old: Mayor, I do hope you'll forgive us. It has been a long road, and I find I am dreadfully tired. Darling, shall we go up and see this gift of yours?
new: Forgive us, Mayor, the long road has left me dreadfully tired. Darling, shall we go up and see this gift of yours?

speaker: adela_druskenvald
old: Oh, swell. Philly, don't pout, the house will be darling. Friends, you'll come to dinner tomorrow, won't you, once we've seen the rooms?
new: Oh, swell. Philly, don't pout, the house will be darling. Friends, come to dinner tomorrow once we've seen the rooms, won't you?

speaker: Narrator
old: Phillip's smile has been put on a half-beat late, and the hand on his cane is white at the knuckles. He is looking at the oak.
new: Phillip's smile comes a half-beat late, his knuckles white on his cane as he stares at the oak.

speaker: phillip_druskenvald
old: Splendid. Forty gold between you for the inn, on me. The estate, tomorrow evening, and we shall have a grand old time.
new: Splendid. Forty gold between you for the inn, on me. Tomorrow evening at the estate, we'll have a grand old time.

speaker: Narrator
old: You watch two small figures, one twirling a cane, walk up the winding path toward the crooked manor on its hill, the windows lit and every line askew.
new: Two small figures, one twirling a cane, walk the winding path up to the lit, crooked manor on the hill.

speaker: Narrator
old: In the round below, the oak's carved faces lie in the moonlight, and one of them, you would swear, turns to watch them go.
new: Below, moonlight catches the oak's carved faces, and you'd swear one turns to watch them go.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: Oh, thank the moon you are strangers! I dropped three unsigned letters into the wrong cubbies, and if Miss Theodora sorts the dead-letter sack tonight, I shall die a second time.
new: Thank the moon you're strangers! I put three unsigned letters in the wrong cubbies. If Miss Theodora sorts the dead-letter sack tonight, I'll die a second time.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: They were meant for Deputy Butterman. Now one sits on Constable Squire's desk, one went to the undertaker, and the square goat has the third. Please fetch them back.
new: They're for Deputy Butterman. Now one's on Constable Squire's desk, one's with the undertaker, and the square goat has the third. Please fetch them back.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: Constable Squire has eyes like carpentry nails, and Mr. Shade measures your collarbone whenever you say good evening. If I go near either of them, my knees will turn to suet.
new: Constable Squire has eyes like carpentry nails, and Mr. Shade measures your collarbone whenever you say good evening. Near either of them, my knees turn to suet.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: Bless your boots! Look for lavender paper sealed with a crooked heart, and please do not read the bit about his ears.
new: Bless your boots! Look for lavender paper sealed with a crooked heart, and please don't read the bit about his ears.

speaker: Narrator
old: {name} slides two fingers across the green blotter, and the lavender sheet vanishes into a coat pocket without a rustle.
new: {name} slides two fingers across the green blotter, pocketing the lavender sheet without a rustle.

speaker: doris_squire
old: Take it. I read it twice to see if it was a cipher from the woods. It is badly spelled. I mean it kindly.
new: Take it. I read it twice checking for a woods cipher. Badly spelled, I mean that kindly.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Unclaimed things come to me sooner or later, one way or another. I kept the lilac note in the third drawer, just in case.
new: Unclaimed things come to me sooner or later. I kept the lilac note in the third drawer, just in case.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Paper is light, but keeping secrets takes drawer space. Leave five coins for the ledger and give me a cousin's middle name for my list, and we are square.
new: Keeping secrets takes drawer space. Leave five coins for the ledger and a cousin's middle name for my list, and we're square.

speaker: Narrator
old: The tether chain clinks against the founder's stone as the old billy goat works his jaw sideways. A corner of lavender paper sticks out from his beard.
new: The old billy goat's tether clinks against the founder's stone as he chews, a corner of lavender paper sticking from his beard.

speaker: Narrator
old: {name} scratches behind the goat's horned crown until his yellow eyes half-close, then draws the damp last third of the page from his teeth.
new: {name} scratches behind the goat's horns until his yellow eyes half-close, then pulls the damp last third of the page from his teeth.

speaker: Narrator
old: The billy goat fixes {name} with a flat yellow stare, gives one final chew, and swallows the last scrap with great dignity.
new: The billy goat fixes {name} with a flat yellow stare, chews once, and swallows the last scrap with great dignity.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: One from the desk, one from the parlor, and one mostly inside the goat. At least Miss Theodora will not pin them to the noticeboard.
new: One from the desk, one from the parlor, one mostly inside the goat. At least Miss Theodora won't pin them to the noticeboard.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: Only now I am looking at them, and my courage has gone cold. What on earth do I do about Howie?
new: Now my courage has gone cold. What on earth do I do about Howie?

speaker: howie_butterman
old: For me? Well now, nobody ever compared my ears to buttercup petals before. I am not sure it is accurate, Miss Geneva, but I am mighty pleased.
new: For me? Nobody ever compared my ears to buttercup petals before. Not sure it's accurate, Miss Geneva, but I'm mighty pleased.

speaker: Narrator
old: {name} matches the looping clerk-hand at the bottom of the page, signing it simply from a friend in the post office.
new: {name} matches the looping clerk-hand at the bottom, signing it from a friend in the post office.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: That is neat enough to pass Miss Theodora herself. He will wonder next time he buys a stamp, and that is half the fun.
new: Neat enough to pass Miss Theodora herself. He'll wonder next time he buys a stamp, and that's half the fun.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: Oh dear, the ink has blotted right through the paper. If I send that, he will think a spider died on the page.
new: Oh dear, the ink blotted right through. He'll think a spider died on the page.

speaker: Narrator
old: The lavender scraps curl into black ash over the post office brazier, smelling briefly of cheap scent and sealing wax.
new: The lavender scraps curl into black ash over the brazier, smelling briefly of cheap scent and wax.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
old: There. Better ash than poached eggs in cream, honestly. Tomorrow I shall buy thick cream paper and write him something sensible.
new: Better ash than poached eggs in cream. Tomorrow I'll buy thick cream paper and write him something sensible.

speaker: Narrator
old: Bundles of dried yarrow and bog-mint brush your shoulders, and glass vials clink softly on crooked shelves. Morgan looks up with faraway green eyes, fingers stained violet with crushed roots.
new: Dried yarrow and bog-mint brush your shoulders as vials clink on crooked shelves. Morgan looks up with faraway green eyes and root-stained violet fingers.

speaker: morgan
old: Oh, come in, mind the low beam by the door. I was just labelling the willow-water, or perhaps I already finished that an hour ago.
new: Come in, mind the low beam. I was just labelling the willow-water, unless I finished that an hour ago.

speaker: morgan
old: The red bottles mend torn flesh properly, and the herb bundles mostly comfort the locals, though comfort does half the curing.
new: Red bottles mend torn flesh, and herb bundles comfort the locals, though comfort does half the curing.

speaker: morgan
old: I have no beds for the sick, only bottles and poultices to carry home. People tell me their aches, and I try to remember which jar eased them last time.
new: I only have bottles and poultices to carry home. People tell me their aches, and I try to remember which jar eased them last time.

speaker: morgan
old: Everyone in the hollow has an old name and an older grave to tend. Sometimes I wonder what sort of name I had before the moor took me in.
new: Everyone in the hollow has an old name and an older grave to tend. I wonder what name I had before the moor took me in.

speaker: morgan
old: Some nights I brew tinctures that let a drinker see through mist or hear what the dead whisper in the thatch. I never quite recall who taught me the measure.
new: Some nights I brew tinctures to see through mist or hear the dead whisper in the thatch. I never recall who taught me the measure.

speaker: Narrator
old: The open ledger on Morgan's counter has whole pages torn short, with ink trails stopping mid-word as if the hand simply froze.
new: The open ledger on the counter has pages torn short, ink trails stopping mid-word as if the hand froze.

speaker: morgan
old: Funny thing, the clock strikes one bell and when I blink it is striking the next. I woke here small and alone, and the years between still slip through my fingers.
new: The clock strikes one bell, I blink, and it strikes the next. I woke here small and alone, and the years still slip through my fingers.

speaker: Narrator
old: The parlor smells of beeswax and cold tin. Mori pulls open a shallow cedar drawer filled with gleaming brass coffin plates.
new: The parlor smells of beeswax and cold tin. Mori opens a cedar drawer of brass coffin plates.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Forgive the clutter, friends. I stencil these for the Order of the Oak, though the folks named on them are still walking the streets.
new: I stencil these for the Order of the Oak, though the folks named on them still walk the streets.

speaker: mori_shade
old: I truly could not say. On the first of each month, a folded slip and a silver piece wait beneath my door.
new: On the first of each month, a folded slip and a silver piece wait beneath my door.

speaker: mori_shade
old: A man must keep his fires lit, so I oil my punches and I do not watch the threshold.
new: A man must keep his fires lit, so I oil my punches and do not watch the threshold.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Geneva Fairchild, Howie Butterman, Ambrose Quill, and Finneas Trout. The fifth plate was ordered polished, but left completely blank.
new: Geneva Fairchild, Howie Butterman, Ambrose Quill, Finneas Trout. The fifth was ordered polished, but left blank.

speaker: mori_shade
old: My hands shake more with every letter I strike. You are strangers here, unburdened by our customs: tell me what ought to be done.
new: My hands shake with every letter. You are strangers, unburdened by our customs: tell me what to do.

speaker: Narrator
old: Word travels the cobbled lanes faster than mist off the moor, leaving shuttered windows and bolted doors behind it.
new: Word travels the lanes faster than moor mist, leaving shuttered windows and bolted doors behind.

speaker: mori_shade
old: They cross the mud to avoid my shop now, whispering that the undertaker wishes them cold. Perhaps they are right to fear me.
new: They cross the mud to avoid my shop, whispering the undertaker wishes them cold. Perhaps they are right.

speaker: Narrator
old: Brass curls and blackens in the belly of the iron stove, filling the small room with a sharp, metallic tang.
new: Brass curls and blackens in the iron stove, filling the room with a sharp metallic tang.

speaker: Narrator
old: Constable Squire turns the paper over once in her gloved fingers, her face as grey and unreadable as slate.
new: Constable Squire turns the paper in her gloved fingers, her face grey as slate.

speaker: doris_squire
old: Keep your shop shuttered after the third bell, Mori. I will copy these into the ledger and walk the Round myself.
new: Keep your shop shuttered after the third bell, Mori. I will copy these into the ledger and walk the Round.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Best to let the village sleep easy, I suppose. I will have the oil lamp trimmed before the next slip arrives.
new: Best let the village sleep easy. I will have the lamp trimmed before the next slip arrives.

speaker: Narrator
old: A single brass plate rests upon the workbench, newly struck, the metal filings still clinging to the letters.
new: A newly struck brass plate rests on the workbench, metal filings still clinging to the letters.

speaker: mori_shade
old: The monthly note came while you were at that dreadful house, friends. They finally gave me a name for the blank plate, and I thought you should see it.
new: The monthly note came while you were at that dreadful house. They finally gave me a name for the blank plate.

speaker: Narrator
old: The scent of dried rosemary and freshly turned peat clings to the woman in black. Her white hair gleams like bone under the lantern light.
new: Dried rosemary and fresh peat cling to the woman in black, her white hair gleaming like bone.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Step softly, newly arrived. You stand upon ground that has welcomed many before you, and will hold many more before the moon wanes.
new: Step softly, newly arrived. This ground has welcomed many, and will hold many more before the moon wanes.

speaker: mori_shade
old: When a companion falls in Druskenvald, the soil does not easily let them go. I wash the brow, fold the hands, and pay the earth its proper due.
new: Druskenvald's soil does not easily let the fallen go. I wash the brow, fold the hands, and pay the earth its due.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Old Yorgrim down at the cemetery taught me the spade-work when I first woke here. Every soul deserves a quiet pillow, whatever they were before.
new: Old Yorgrim at the cemetery taught me the spade-work. Every soul deserves a quiet pillow.

speaker: mori_shade
old: The Mayor's folk feed the Oak of Many Faces with blood, while the Brightsingers try to sing the dark away. I keep to the Strangers' way: we owe the Ferryman a polite nod and a clean ledger.
new: The Mayor's folk feed the Oak of Many Faces blood, and the Brightsingers sing at the dark. We Strangers just owe the Ferryman a nod and a clean ledger.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Do not pluck the white violets that grow round the base of the Founder's Round. Their roots drink deep from those who died without a name, and they weep on your fingers.
new: Do not pluck the white violets round the Founder's Round. Their roots drink from the nameless dead, and weep on your fingers.

speaker: mori_shade
old: You know the Vagrant's mark, then. He rowed us all across the dark water once, and he watches still to see if we waste the second breath he gave us.
new: You know the Vagrant's mark. He rowed us across the dark water once, and watches to see if we waste our second breath.

speaker: mori_shade
old: It is only an old keepsake from the riverbank, traveller. A reminder that every road ends at the water's edge.
new: Just a riverbank keepsake, traveller. A reminder that every road ends at the water's edge.

speaker: Narrator
old: The parlor goes awful still save for the dry rustle of pages as she turns to a black ledger on the desk, smellin' of cedar and cold tallow.
new: The parlor goes awful still save for dry pages rustlin' as she opens a black ledger smellin' of cedar and cold tallow.

speaker: mori_shade
old: I do not call the departed back myself. I only go down to the water, ask the Ferryman to turn his oar, and carry him his toll.
new: I do not call the dead back myself. I only carry the Ferryman his toll and ask him to turn his oar.

speaker: mori_shade
old: He turns his oar only for souls in the water no more than ten days. They return weak and stumbling for ten days, the water's shadow clinging on.
new: He turns it only for souls dead ten days or less, and they return weak for ten days with the water's shadow on them.

speaker: mori_shade
old: The toll is a thousand gold pieces for each soul I carry to him, whoever they were and however far they came. I keep no gems and ask no other payment.
new: The toll is a thousand gold pieces each, whoever they were. I ask no other payment.

speaker: mori_shade
old: You will see the toll set out for each companion before anything is paid. Tell me whom you mean to call back to the near shore.
new: You will see each companion's toll before paying. Tell me whom to call back to the near shore.

speaker: mori_shade
old: The Ferryman keeps his ledger open, and the offer stands for the full ten days, whenever your purse allows.
new: The Ferryman's ledger stays open for the full ten days, whenever your purse allows.

speaker: mori_shade
old: The Midnight and Witching hours I give to the graves, and the Ferryman takes no asking now.
new: The Midnight and Witching hours belong to the graves. The Ferryman takes no asking now.

speaker: mori_shade
old: Come back to me from the Twilight Hour until the Evening Hour is spent. The ten days will keep.
new: Come back between the Twilight and Evening hours. The ten days will keep.

speaker: Narrator
old: The tang of cold tallow and wet dog hangs about her apron. She keeps her head down, paring grey fat from a knucklebone with a notched knife.
new: Cold tallow and wet dog hang about her apron as she pares grey fat from a knucklebone.

speaker: mrs_oakum
old: If you want prime cuts, talk to the master up front. I only scrape the troughs and haul the bone-bucket out back.
new: Talk to the master up front for prime cuts. I only scrape troughs and haul the bone-bucket out back.

speaker: mrs_oakum
old: It suits me fine. Folks leave me be, and I get the gristle and marrow-ends to carry home before the Evening bell rings.
new: Folks leave me be, and I get the gristle and marrow-ends to carry home before the Evening bell.

speaker: mrs_oakum
old: Folk here pray to their big thirsty tree and think the hedges will keep the dark out. A fence only keeps in what wants to stay.
new: Folk pray to their thirsty tree and trust the hedges. A fence only keeps in what wants to stay.

speaker: mrs_oakum
old: Something foul is seeping out of the Skitterdeep mine, up north-west in the crags. The creek water tastes of copper and bad fever, and the beasts know it.
new: Foul water seeps from Skitterdeep mine, north-west in the crags. The creek tastes of copper and bad fever, and the beasts know it.

speaker: Narrator
old: Coarse grey hairs bristle along the scarred skin of her forearms, and her breath catches at the scent of raw liver on the block.
new: Coarse grey hairs bristle on her scarred forearms, and her breath catches at raw liver on the block.

speaker: mrs_oakum
old: Keep your eyes to yourself, stranger. A heavy chain and a sack of butcher's offal is all that keeps my teeth out of this town come dark.
new: Eyes to yourself, stranger. Only a heavy chain and butcher's offal keep my teeth out of this town come dark.

speaker: Narrator
old: She smells of starch and dried chamomile, her hands folded neat over her apron while her gaze flicks toward the nursery stairs.
new: Smelling of starch and chamomile, she folds her hands over her apron and glances toward the nursery stairs.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
old: Good evening. If you are looking for Wendel, he keeps his hours in the office, though I ask that you keep your voices low near little Rose's door.
new: Wendel is in the office, though please keep your voices low near little Rose's door.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
old: Being the mayor's wife means keeping the silver bright and making sure Wendel does not promise the parish away to flatter quality. My real work is keeping Rose at her lessons and indoors.
new: I keep the silver bright and stop Wendel promising the parish away to flatter quality, but my real work is keeping Rose indoors at her lessons.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
old: It is a respectable village when folk mind their own hearths. I tell Wendel that all this fuss over old trees and midnight bells only gives the simple folk bad dreams.
new: Folk should mind their own hearths. I tell Wendel this fuss over old trees and midnight bells only gives simple folk bad dreams.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
old: Too many shutters have stayed barred past the third bell this month. The baker's apprentice has a rattle in his chest that no kettle of broth seems to touch.
new: Too many shutters stay barred past the third bell, and no broth touches the rattle in the baker's apprentice's chest.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
old: People do not just wander off into the gorse when they know the paths from birth, no matter what the constable writes down. I bolt Rose's shutters before the first bell, and I do not open them for anyone.
new: Folk who know the paths from birth do not just wander into the gorse, whatever the constable writes. I bolt Rose's shutters before the first bell for good.

speaker: Narrator
old: Dark sap weeps from the knots of the old oak as a dozen wooden eyelids creak open in the moonlight. The smell of iron and wet earth rises from the roots, and the carved mouths begin to move together.
new: Dark sap weeps from the old oak as a dozen wooden eyelids creak open. Iron and wet earth rise from the roots as carved mouths move together.

speaker: Narrator
old: A dry chorus rustles through the bark like dead leaves scraping across a stone floor. They whisper that their roots are parched, that they are so very tired of the dark, and that the axe took them for crimes they never did.
new: A dry chorus rustles like dead leaves on stone: their roots are parched, they are tired of the dark, and the axe took them for crimes they never did.

speaker: Narrator
old: Three faces near the base of the trunk strain forward against the grain, speaking one after another in hushed, splintered breaths. A hollow-cheeked woman claims she only took a loaf of barley bread, while a gaunt man swears the boundary stone was moved before he ever plowed the field.
new: Three faces near the base strain forward in splintered breaths. A gaunt woman claims she only took barley bread; a man swears the boundary stone was moved before he plowed.

speaker: Narrator
old: You snarl the villain's curses to the rafters, and the whole taproom rises in a roar of boots and tankards as the curtain falls.
new: You snarl the villain's curses, and the taproom roars with boots and tankards as the curtain falls.

speaker: Narrator
old: The candles along the stage are pinched out one by one, leaving the smell of tallow and cold dust while the actors pack their trunks in silence.
new: The stage candles are pinched out, leaving tallow and cold dust while the actors pack in silence.

speaker: Narrator
old: A chain and a padlock hold the gate, and a board nailed across it says BY ORDER OF THE MAYOR. On the step behind lies one small child's shoe, laces still tied.
new: A padlocked chain and a board marked BY ORDER OF THE MAYOR hold the gate. Behind it lies a child's shoe, laces still tied.

speaker: Narrator
old: The house leans over a lane of empty ones. When you look at its windows, it seems to have been looking at you a moment before.
new: The house leans over an empty lane, its windows watching you just before you look up.

speaker: Narrator
old: Nobody who lives on the lane will say it plainly. A woman at her gate says the children dare each other, a boy at the inn says the house has more rooms inside than it has outside, and everyone says the shoe belongs to somebody.
new: A neighbour says children dare each other, a boy at the inn says the house has more rooms inside than out, and everyone says the shoe is somebody's.

speaker: Narrator
old: The shoe on the step is gone. Behind you, in the lane, a child laughs, and nobody is there. You pull the gate shut and press the chain back round it, and it feels like the right thing to have done.
new: The shoe is gone. An unseen child laughs in the lane behind you, and you pull the gate shut and chain it back up.

speaker: Narrator
old: A scrap of herb-stained parchment hangs crookedly from the apothecary door, smelling faintly of crushed mint.
new: Herb-stained parchment hangs crookedly from the apothecary door, smelling of mint.

speaker: morgan
old: If anyone has a spare moment, a pedlar in the Round is selling a plague cure. I cannot leave the kettle, so please see what is in it, and whether it does harm.
new: A pedlar in the Round is selling a plague cure. I cannot leave the kettle, so please see what is in it and whether it does harm.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
old: Step lively, good neighbours, and fortify your humours with Pennywhistle's Sovereign Specific. Every green bottle carries a fresh guarantee against the creeping itch, or your brass Cheerfully refunded.
new: Fortify your humours with Pennywhistle's Sovereign Specific! Every green bottle is guaranteed against the creeping itch, or your brass cheerfully refunded.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
old: Now, I could hardly hand over my sainted grandmother's receipt in the open damp. Call it forty mountain herbs steeped under a lucky star, and leave the arithmetic to me.
new: I cannot hand over my grandmother's receipt here. Call it forty mountain herbs steeped under a lucky star.

speaker: Narrator
old: The cork gives with a sticky pop, releasing a warm, unmistakable waft of cellar cider and cheap cinnamon.
new: The cork pops, releasing a warm waft of cellar cider and cheap cinnamon.

speaker: Narrator
old: Barnaby straightens his cuffs by the crate of clinking bottles, watching the crowd with bright, restless eyes.
new: Barnaby straightens his cuffs by the clinking bottles, watching the crowd with restless eyes.

speaker: Narrator
old: Beneath the sweet orchard cider and cinnamon bark sits a bitter trace of boiled willow and wildflower honey. It will cure no plague, though it might soothe a feverish throat and warm a cold belly.
new: Beneath the cider and cinnamon sits boiled willow and honey. It will cure no plague, only soothe a throat and warm a belly.

speaker: Narrator
old: The draught burns pleasantly across your tongue with fierce cinnamon and sour apples, masking whatever else might be floating at the bottom.
new: Fierce cinnamon and sour apples burn your tongue, masking whatever floats at the bottom.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
old: Keep your voice down, I beg you, before the sick folk lose their temper. It is mulled cider, willow bark for the aches, and a spoonful of honey to keep their spirits from sinking.
new: Keep your voice down before the sick folk lose their temper. It is mulled cider, willow bark for aches, and honey for their spirits.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
old: Bless your heart, I have faced louder bailiffs in three counties and sold them all hair tonic. Take two bottles for three coins and spare us both the frown.
new: I have sold hair tonic to louder bailiffs in three counties. Take two bottles for three coins and spare us the frown.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
old: Well, you have the measure of my little kettle now. A drop of warmth and willow tea is better than cold panic, so what do you mean to do with me?
new: Warmth and willow tea beat cold panic. What do you mean to do with me?

speaker: Narrator
old: Word travels fast around the blankets, and within moments a chorus of coughing townsfolk is pelting Barnaby's cart toward the gate with turnip tops.
new: Word travels fast, and soon coughing townsfolk are pelting Barnaby's cart toward the gate with turnip tops.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
old: You have a gentle soul beneath that travel dust, friend. Take the best bottle from the bottom row for the apothecary, and take this coin for keeping a quiet tongue.
new: Take the bottom-row bottle for the apothecary, friend, and this coin for a quiet tongue.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
old: Now there is a head for honest commerce in a dark season. Stand beside the crate looking healthy, nod when I mention the forty herbs, and we shall split the evening's tin.
new: Stand by the crate looking healthy, nod at the forty herbs, and we shall split the evening's tin.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
old: No offence meant, my dear colleague, but a trade secret shared with four strangers is just a recipe on a tavern wall.
new: No offence, colleague, but a secret shared with four strangers is just a recipe on a tavern wall.

speaker: Narrator
old: Stacks of damp parchment lean across the mayor's desk like toppling gravestones, smelling faintly of boiled vinegar and sealing wax.
new: Damp parchment leans across the mayor's desk like gravestones, smelling of boiled vinegar and wax.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Dreadful business, friends, dreadful! Half the parish is coughing up centipedes in the taproom, yet I cannot legally bar the inn doors without three county seals in triplicate.
new: Half the parish is coughing up centipedes in the taproom, yet I cannot bar the inn doors without three county seals in triplicate!

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: My hands are tied with red ribbon while the kettle boils over. Would you take the sheaf to Miss Ledger and Miss Mayville for their stamps?
new: Would you take the sheaf to Miss Ledger and Miss Mayville for their stamps?

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Why, one for the parish chest, one for the post bag, and one nailed to the Oak so the Green Queen sees we did things properly.
new: One for the parish chest, one for the post bag, and one nailed to the Oak for the Green Queen.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Bless your brisk boots! Mind the ink does not smudge in the fog, or Miss Ledger will make us start from the first sheet.
new: Bless your brisk boots! Do not smudge the ink in the fog, or Miss Ledger will make us start over.

speaker: Narrator
old: Tamsin Ledger wets her thumb and turns a fresh page, her spectacles gleaming like two brass coins in the lantern light.
new: Tamsin Ledger turns a page, her spectacles gleaming like brass coins.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
old: Form Seven-B, Emergency Pestilence and Bedstead Tally. What a treat! I can countersign the second copy the moment we verify the active cots in the common room.
new: Form Seven-B, Emergency Pestilence and Bedstead Tally! I can countersign once we verify the active cots in the common room.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
old: Fifteen? No, no, the drover under the settle is only sleeping off turnip gin. I have struck him from the pestilence column in red ink.
new: Fifteen? The drover under the settle is only sleeping off turnip gin. I have struck him in red ink.

speaker: Narrator
old: Behind the wicket, Theodora Mayville sorts dead letters with a bone knife, her head tilting in sharp, birdlike jerks.
new: Behind the wicket, Theodora Mayville sorts dead letters with a bone knife, her head tilting like a bird's.

speaker: theodora_mayville
old: The Mayor's quarantine circulars. Set them by the brass scale and do not breathe on the gummed edges. I stamp emergency notices after the afternoon sorting.
new: The quarantine circulars. Set them by the scale and do not breathe on the gum. I stamp notices after afternoon sorting.

speaker: Narrator
old: She fixes you with a round, unblinking stare and drives the postmark into the wax with a single sharp peck of her wrist.
new: With an unblinking stare, she drives the postmark into the wax with a sharp peck of her wrist.

speaker: theodora_mayville
old: Properly witnessed, properly weighed. Take your papers off my counter before you shed road grit into the pigeonholes.
new: Properly witnessed and weighed. Take your papers before you shed road grit into the pigeonholes.

speaker: theodora_mayville
old: Haste is how envelopes lose their corners. Come back when the kettle has cooled and I have finished the dead-letter bundle.
new: Haste ruins envelopes. Come back when the kettle cools and the dead letters are sorted.

speaker: Narrator
old: While her back is turned to the sorting rack, {name} rolls a carved cork in purple ink and presses three neat rings across the parchment.
new: While her back is turned, {name} inks a carved cork and presses three purple rings onto the parchment.

speaker: Narrator
old: A heavy gloved hand closes on {name}'s wrist just as the counterfeit stamp leaves a smeared purple crescent on the page.
new: A gloved hand grabs {name}'s wrist as the fake stamp smears purple on the page.

speaker: doris_squire
old: Counterfeiting the parish postmark during a pestilence. Keep the smudged copy for the Mayor, and bring your boots to the cells until morning.
new: Counterfeiting the postmark during a pestilence. Keep the smudged copy for the Mayor, and come to the cells until morning.

speaker: Narrator
old: Wendel presses his own brass signet into the warm wax, then holds all three sheets up to the hearth like prize marrow squashes.
new: Wendel presses his brass signet into the wax and holds the three sheets up like prize squashes.

speaker: wendel_somerton
old: Three ribbons, nine stamps, and not a single blot on the margin! Now the village may be Deathly Ill in full compliance with the bylaws.
new: Three ribbons, nine stamps, and no blots! Now the village may be Deathly Ill in full compliance with the bylaws.

speaker: ambrose_quill
old: Ah, fresh ears in the Green Queen's taproom! I am Ambrose Quill, humble vessel of the muse, paring eternity down to metre and ink.
new: Fresh ears! I am Ambrose Quill, humble vessel of the muse, paring eternity down to metre and ink.

speaker: ambrose_quill
old: Mayor Somerton commissioned an anthem for the Founders' table, yet the village's own name resists my craft. What mortal tongue can rhyme with Wickermoor?
new: Mayor Somerton commissioned an anthem for the Founders' table, yet what mortal tongue can rhyme with Wickermoor?
